compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model.context: Part of a holiday experiment that compiled an incident-triage SOP into a 3B model. The code is at arpitbbhayani/workflow-slm.

compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model--curate.how: QLoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct: 4-bit NF4 quantization, LoRA r=16 and alpha=32 on all linear layers, three epochs, under four hours on one RTX 3060. The 115 MB adapter replaced a 3,500-token SOP in the system prompt.
steps: Pick a workflow that is a stable finite state machine.
Build a deterministic simulator with known root causes.
Generate multi-turn traces with an oracle and validate them.
Fine-tune a small model with QLoRA and masked loss.
Evaluate on held-out scenarios against a frontier model.

compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model--curate.how: Count the SOP tokens that are resent on every turn, not just the one-time prompt size. A 3,500-token SOP over five turns is about 5,200 input tokens per request.
steps: Measure the current prompt size per turn.
Multiply it by the average number of turns per task.
Compare that recurring cost with compiling or caching the procedure.

compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model--curate.how: Move the procedure out of the prompt and into an adapter. The system prompt becomes a versioned trigger such as `incident_triage_v1`; the weights carry the state machine.
steps: Define a stable, versioned trigger name.
Train the adapter on the full procedure and its tool calls.
At inference, send only the trigger plus the current input and tools.
Version the adapter when the procedure changes.

compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model--curate.how: In the dataset collator, label user alerts, system triggers and tool responses with `-100`, so the loss is computed only on assistant actions.
steps: Identify the assistant-action spans in every trace.
Set every other token label to -100.
Verify that gradients only flow through decisions.
Compare with an unmasked baseline to confirm the difference.

compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model--curate.how: A deterministic simulator with 12 microservices and 9 root causes, plus an oracle that knows the optimal path, generated 5,116 multi-turn conversations; every trace passed eight programmatic checks.
Prompts are editable at runtime; compiled weights require retraining or a new adapter version. Use compilation only when the procedure is stable and high-volume.
steps: Estimate how often the workflow changes.
If it changes weekly, keep it in the prompt.
If it is stable and high-volume, compile it.
Keep a versioned fallback prompt for edge cases.

compiling-an-sop-into-a-3b-model--curate.how: Store the procedure in the adapter and keep a stable trigger in the prompt; treat prompt text and model weights as two places the same workflow can live.
steps: Write down the procedure as a finite state machine.
Decide whether it changes often enough to need prompt editing.
If it is stable, compile it into an adapter and leave a trigger token.
Keep a prompt-based fallback for edge cases.

slop-debt.context: From an essay on how LLM-generated codebases fail. It is the author's observation, not a formal study.

slop-debt--curated-1.how: Audit how much of the codebase was generated without a human architectural decision, and whether anyone can explain why it has that shape.
steps: Sample recent merged pull requests.
Ask who chose the structure, not just who approved it.
Look for locally correct but globally inconsistent patterns.
Measure incoherence, not just volume.

slop-debt--curated-2.how: For any piece of debt, ask what decision produced it. If no decision exists, it is slop.
steps: Pick a confusing module.
Trace it to a design decision or a person.
If neither exists, classify it as slop.
Use the distinction to decide whether to refactor or rewrite.

slop-debt--curated-3.how: The model reads the existing code as context on every generation pass, so inconsistent patterns become the examples it copies.
steps: Check whether generated code is used as context for later generation.
Look for the same problem solved multiple ways.
Add a human-owned architectural reference before more generation.
Stop generation passes that learn from unreviewed slop.

slop-debt--curated-4.how: A diff-level review catches local mistakes; slop is globally inconsistent but locally plausible, so it passes review.
steps: Review for fit with existing patterns, not just correctness.
Ask why this shape was chosen.
Compare against a reference architecture.
Use a human architectural review for generated modules.

slop-debt--curated-5.how: Slop is spread across the codebase at low intensity, so cleaning one module does not change the system's overall shape.
steps: Map where the incoherence is concentrated.
Check whether neighboring modules are still generating new patterns.
Decide whether incremental refactoring can change the system's shape.
Escalate to a rewrite if it cannot.

slop-debt--curated-6.how: A human-owned rewrite: define the target architecture first, then use the model inside that shape.

ai-first-org.context: From an essay on how AI-first engineering orgs change planning, review, hiring and metrics.

ai-first-org--curated-1.how: Measure where engineering time goes after coding gets faster; the gating step is the new bottleneck.
steps: Measure where engineering time goes now.
Identify the step that gates delivery.
Redesign process around verification, not typing.

ai-first-org--curated-2.how: Run planning as a just-in-time decision: prototype first, get user feedback, and write a doc only when reversal is expensive.

ai-first-org--curated-3.how: Before asking a person, ask the model to gather context from git history, CODEOWNERS, recent commits and the PR discussion.
steps: Write down what you actually need to know before asking a person.
Ask the model for git history, ownership or decision context first.
Escalate only the judgment calls the model cannot make.
Turn questions you ask repeatedly into a standing job.

ai-first-org--curated-4.how: Split review by reversibility and judgment: AI owns style, bugs and tests; humans own security, legal and product risk.
steps: Ask whether a wrong call is expensive to reverse.
Ask whether it needs risk-tolerance judgment.
If both answers are no, skip the human gate.
Revisit the split monthly as models improve.

ai-first-org--curated-5.how: Hire for the two profiles that remain scarce: product-minded builders and engineers with deep systems expertise.
steps: Define the systems constraints the model cannot handle.
Look for product sense in builders.
Test for judgment, not raw coding throughput.

ai-first-org--curated-6.how: Track AI-assisted commit percentage as an activity metric, never as the outcome.
steps: Track onboarding ramp time.
Track pull-request cycle time.
Track the share of AI-assisted commits.
Pair them with retention, incidents or adoption.

ai-first-org--curated-7.how: Pick the workflow the team dreads most and ask whether it still closes the gap it was created for.

three-skills.context: From a proposal for three org-level Claude skills: create-service, deploy and debug.

three-skills--curated-1.how: Compare a stale doc with a broken tool: the doc fails silently, the tool fails in front of the next user and gets fixed.
steps: Find a doc that is known to be stale.
Replace the critical path with an executable check.
Let the failure surface in the workflow.

three-skills--curated-2.how: The three skills are the repeated org workflows: create a service, deploy and roll back, debug an incident.
steps: List the three workflows in your org.
Identify where people wait or guess.
Encode the repeated parts as tools.

three-skills--curated-3.how: Start with debugging because incidents create immediate, verifiable demand for the tool.

three-skills--curated-4.how: Build deployment with the rollback path exercised as often as the forward path.

three-skills--curated-5.how: Create-service touches the most infrastructure, so a half-built version relocates confusion instead of removing it.
steps: Map the provisioning steps.
Automate database, logging, identity and deploy.
Ship it only when the full path works end to end.

three-skills--curated-6.how: Pick one metric per tool that is cheap to measure and hard to argue with.

g-eval.context: From an explainer on the 2023 G-Eval paper by Yang Liu and coauthors at Microsoft.

g-eval--curated-1.how: Combine a precise rubric, a model-generated chain-of-thought, and token-probability scoring.
steps: Define the evaluation dimension.
Generate the evaluation steps.
Score with token probabilities.
Calibrate against human labels.

g-eval--curated-2.how: Use G-Eval when there is no gold reference; define the criterion and let the judge evaluate against it.
steps: Check whether a reference answer exists.
If not, write a precise criterion.
Use a reference-free judge.

g-eval--curated-3.how: Replace the vague 1–5 prompt with a concrete definition of the dimension and what a good output looks like.
steps: Write a one-paragraph rubric.
Define each score level concretely.
Test it on known good and bad outputs.

g-eval--curated-4.how: Generate the chain-of-thought once per rubric, cache it, and reuse it for every candidate.
steps: Generate evaluation steps from the rubric.
Cache them per rubric version.
Score each candidate with the cached steps.
Read the chain-of-thought when a score looks wrong.

g-eval--curated-5.how: Use a judge from a different model family than the system under test; pin its version and recalibrate.
steps: Identify the model family under test.
Choose a judge from another family.
Pin the judge version.
Recalibrate against human labels.

g-eval--curated-6.how: Use a classifier or parser for a closed-form check; reserve G-Eval for open-ended judgment.

ai-topological-sort.context: From an essay on modeling AI workflows and multi-agent systems as DAGs.

ai-topological-sort--curated-1.how: Model the workflow as a DAG: tasks are nodes, dependencies are edges, and the topological order is the schedule.
steps: List the tasks.
Draw every dependency edge.
Check for cycles.
Compute the topological order.

ai-topological-sort--curated-2.how: Treat an edge as a correctness constraint: the consumer cannot run before the producer finishes.
steps: For each edge, name what breaks if it is reversed.
If nothing breaks, question the edge.
If data is stale or missing, keep it.

ai-topological-sort--curated-3.how: Group nodes by topological level and run each level concurrently.
steps: Compute the DAG levels.
Dispatch each level in parallel.
Join at the merge node.

ai-topological-sort--curated-4.how: On failure, traverse forward from the affected node and reuse cached outputs outside its subgraph.
steps: Mark the affected node.
Traverse its descendants.
Recompute only that subgraph.
Reuse every other cache entry.

ai-topological-sort--curated-5.how: Topological sort gives order, not load balance; profile the critical path and fan-in nodes.
steps: Find the longest dependency chain.
Find high fan-in merge nodes.
Measure where the schedule actually waits.

ai-topological-sort--curated-6.how: If the topological order is shorter than the node count, a cycle exists; reject the workflow at definition time.

ai-topological-sort--curated-7.how: Treat the dependency graph as the spec and the topological order as the scheduler input.
steps: Draw the graph before writing orchestration code.
Separate sequential tasks from independent ones.
Let parallelism and incremental recomputation fall out of the graph.

embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.context: A practical guide to the embedding layer of a production RAG system, covering model selection, chunking, hybrid retrieval, and retrieval evaluation.

embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.how: Compare pipeline variants on a domain-specific golden set instead of picking an encoder from MTEB alone; change chunking and retrieval breadth before blaming the model.
steps: Assemble 100–200 real queries with expected answers.
Measure retrieval quality before touching the encoder.
Test chunk sizes and overlap on that set.

embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.how: Split recursively on paragraph and sentence boundaries, count tokens with the model's tokenizer, and keep 10–20% overlap.
steps: Measure chunk length in tokens, not characters.
Target 256–512 tokens for prose.
Add 10–20% overlap at boundaries.
Check that boundary facts appear whole in at least one chunk.

embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.how: Serialize each row with its column names, or embed the table as a parent and its rows as children.
steps: Inspect how tables are currently flattened.
Repeat headers on every row or write `column: value` pairs.
Use parent-child chunks for large tables.
Run queries that depend on a cell value to confirm retrieval.

steps: Record encoder name and version with each vector.
Reject queries whose encoder does not match the index.
Build a shadow index before switching.
Keep the old index available for rollback.

steps: Index the corpus both densely and lexically.
Retrieve a wide candidate pool from each.
Fuse the lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
Rerank only the top candidates.
Fix recall before adding precision layers.

embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.how: Run the evaluation set through RAGAS, read recall and precision separately, and change the retrieval stage the metric points to.
Hash document content, re-embed only when the hash changes, and delete old chunk IDs before inserting replacements.
steps: Add `last_embedded_at` and a content hash to each document.
Compare the hash before scheduling an embed.
Delete stale chunk IDs through the registry.
Alert when a document's chunks and hash disagree.

temporal-primer.context: A primer on Temporal as a durable execution platform, using a multi-step payment and provisioning flow to explain the programming model and its traps.

temporal-primer--curated-1.how: Model the process as a workflow, put external effects in activities, and let the server persist the event history.
steps: List every step that changes the outside world.
Wrap each in an activity with a retry policy.
Keep ordering and decisions in workflow code.
Test resumption by killing a worker mid-run.

temporal-primer--curated-2.how: Keep clocks, randomness, network calls, and mutable globals out of workflow code; put each external effect in an activity.
steps: Mark every I/O operation as an activity.
Replace `time.now()` and `random.random()` with workflow-safe equivalents.
Keep workers stateless.
Review workflow code for hidden global state.

temporal-primer--curated-3.how: Treat the event history as the source of truth and replay workflows locally after code changes.
steps: Record a history from a test run.
Replay it against the new code.
Fix any command mismatch before deploying.
Add replay tests to CI.

temporal-primer--curated-4.how: Gate changed logic with `get_version` branches, keep old paths until their workflows drain, then remove the gate.
steps: Detect whether the change alters command order or names.
Add a version gate around the new branch.
Deploy and let old workflows finish.
Remove the old branch after the drain.

temporal-primer--curated-5.how: Expose an endpoint that sends the signal, then block the workflow on `wait_condition` with an escalation timeout.
steps: Define the signal payload and sender.
Suspend the workflow on `wait_condition`.
Add a timeout path for escalation.
Verify the wait survives a worker restart.

temporal-primer--curated-6.how: Replace the cron-plus-status-column pattern with a workflow that sleeps and continues in the same execution.
steps: Identify jobs that re-read state on every cron run.
Move the wait into a workflow timer.
Persist state in workflow variables or activities.
Remove the polling scheduler once the timer is live.

temporal-primer--curated-7.how: Pass accumulated state into `continue_as_new` at a fixed event-count threshold while keeping the workflow ID.
steps: Estimate events added per cycle.
Set a threshold around 10,000 events.
Call `continue_as_new` with the current state.
Keep the workflow ID stable for callers.

steps: Log what the index contains for a sample document.
Log which chunks each answer used.

rag-production--curated-2.how: Record the model and version on every chunk, build the replacement index in parallel, compare results, then move the alias.

Shift traffic gradually.

steps: Hash the document body, excluding volatile metadata.

steps: Count prompt tokens per turn.

Summarize or drop old turns.

steps: Choose the required opening token or structure.

steps: Compute the density you need.
Estimate points required as dimension grows.
Compare with available data.

Plot their distance histogram.

Test a lower-dimensional projection if it appears.

Aggregate retrieval counts.

Measure retrieval recall after projection.

Re-test the split every year.

Track whether they are building judgment, not just output.

Persist promises before responding.

steps: Assign a ballot when a leader is elected.

Raise the ballot only on a new election.

Treat a negative as safe to recommend.
Verify positives before suppressing.

Multiply by expected item count.
Leave headroom for growth before resizing.

clock-sync-nightmare.context: From a distributed-systems series on time, covering physical synchronization, logical clocks, and the bounded-uncertainty approach used by Spanner and CockroachDB.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-1.how: Replace the question 'what time is it' with 'what interval is guaranteed to contain the true time' when ordering events matters.
steps: Identify where the system orders events by timestamp.
Ask what clock error that order can tolerate.
Bound the error explicitly.
Choose a mechanism that respects the bound.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-2.how: Treat unsynchronized clocks as a source of error proportional to uptime, and resynchronize far more often than the drift budget allows.
steps: Estimate the drift rate of your hardware.
Decide the maximum tolerable skew.
Sync at intervals well below that threshold.
Alert when skew exceeds the budget.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-3.how: Never use raw wall-clock comparison as the sole ordering signal for writes, builds or traces; add a logical sequence or a bounded-uncertainty check.
steps: Find code that compares timestamps across machines.
List the decisions that comparison drives.
Add a logical counter or version where order matters.
Check traces for impossible sequences.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-4.how: Measure round-trip asymmetry on your network before trusting sub-millisecond NTP claims, and never step a clock backward under a running system.
steps: Measure one-way delay in both directions.
Quantify the asymmetry.
Prefer relative adjustments over absolute jumps.
Keep time monotonic for running processes.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-5.how: Use Lamport counters when you only need a consistent order, and vector clocks when the application must detect conflicting concurrent updates.
steps: Decide whether concurrency detection is required.

Budget the space cost before scaling node count.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-6.how: If you can bound clock error, assign commit timestamps and delay visibility until the bound has elapsed.
steps: Establish a trustworthy time source.

Wait out the uncertainty before acknowledging.

clock-sync-nightmare--curated-8.how: Derive the requirement from transaction duration and ordering needs, then choose the cheapest mechanism that meets it.

heartbeats-in-distributed-systems.context: Part of a distributed-systems series on failure detection, covering timeout tuning, phi accrual, gossip, and partition handling.

Set interval and timeout from those two numbers.
Track false failovers and tune the threshold.

Set timeout at ten times the tail RTT or three intervals, whichever is larger.
Count consecutive missed heartbeats before declaring failure.
Use different thresholds for local and cross-region peers.

heartbeats-in-distributed-systems--curat.how: Multiply node count by heartbeat frequency to get background message rate: 1,000 nodes at 500 ms is 2,000 messages per second. Compare that with application traffic before shortening the interval.

Compare heartbeat volume with application request volume.
Check whether GC pauses or congestion would trip the threshold.
Lengthen intervals for nodes whose failure is not urgent.

Keep the window long enough to cover normal jitter.

Gossip the full list to a small random sample each round.
Merge on receive by taking the highest counter and version.
Size detection windows for convergence delay rather than instant agreement.

Make writes and elections conditional on holding it.
Have the minority side fail closed rather than continue.
Test a real partition and verify only one side commits.

heartbeats-in-distributed-systems--curat.how: Choose push when the monitored node can initiate and crash detection is the main need, pull when the monitor must cross asymmetric networks. Use UDP when losing a heartbeat is tolerable and TCP when the message carries state.

cassandra-writes.context: A write-path deep dive on Apache Cassandra, following a mutation from coordinator selection through replication, consistency, and repair.

cassandra-writes--curated-1.how: The coordinator fans the mutation out to all replicas in parallel immediately, then counts acknowledgements until the requested consistency level is met. Replication always happens; the level only controls when the client is told success.
steps: Choose the consistency level from the read pattern, not the write alone.

Measure p99 at each consistency level you offer.

Use NetworkTopologyStrategy for multi-datacenter keyspaces.
Set per-datacenter replica counts deliberately.
Verify replicas land on separate racks where possible.

cassandra-writes--curated-3.how: Append the mutation to the CommitLog, apply it to the sorted MemTable, ack, then flush the frozen MemTable to an immutable SSTable and release the matching log segments. Updates are new timestamped entries reconciled at read time.
steps: Keep the CommitLog on fast local disk.
Size MemTable thresholds against available RAM.

Schedule compaction so SSTables do not pile up.

Use QUORUM or LOCAL_QUORUM as the default for reads and writes.
Reserve ONE for throughput-tolerant workloads.
Avoid ALL where any single replica failure must not stop writes.

cassandra-writes--curated-5.how: When a replica is unreachable but quorum is met, the coordinator writes a hint into a system table and replays it on the node's return, up to `max_hint_window_in_ms` (three hours by default). Beyond that, run `nodetool repair`.
steps: Check the hint window against your longest expected outage.
Alert when a node has been down past the window.
Schedule regular repairs weekly or monthly.
Confirm reads above ONE can trigger read repair.

cassandra-writes--curated-6.how: Every mutation carries a microsecond timestamp and the highest value wins. The coordinator assigns one from its clock when the client omits it, so clock sync directly determines which write survives.
steps: Run NTP on every node and alert on drift.
Keep drift under 500 ms.
Either always set `USING TIMESTAMP` or never set it.
Audit client code for mixed timestamp sources.

cassandra-writes--curated-7.how: Choose partition keys that spread writes, avoid counters or update-heavy tables keyed on one value, and use TTL instead of deletes. Batch only statements that share a partition, and prefer unlogged batches when atomicity is not required.
steps: Review the busiest tables for single-key write patterns.
Add a bucketing component to hot partition keys.
Use TTL for expiring data rather than DELETE.
Restrict batches to one partition and skip the batch log when possible.

redis-replication.context: An internals piece on Redis replication that argues for its push-based design and the operational knobs that come with it.

redis-replication--curated-1.how: Every write executed on the master is appended to the replication backlog and pushed into each replica's output buffer inside the same event-loop iteration, with no per-replica polling or background coordination.
steps: State the replication lag your application can tolerate.
Compare push lag with what a poll interval would give you.
Budget master memory per replica before scaling replica count.
Monitor offsets rather than assuming the model is free.

redis-replication--curated-2.how: A replica issues `PSYNC`; the master forks an RDB snapshot, buffers concurrent writes, transfers the snapshot, replays the buffer, then streams each new write. The backlog keeps recent commands so a brief disconnect resumes at an offset.
steps: Size `repl-backlog-size` for your write throughput and outage length.
Watch for repeated full resyncs as a sign the backlog is too small.
Keep replica connections stable to avoid snapshot churn.
Monitor `master_repl_offset` against `slave_repl_offset`.

redis-replication--curated-3.how: Count what each model costs: pull pays a round trip per replica per interval even when idle; push pays a connection, an output buffer, and backlog bookkeeping per replica on every write.
steps: Estimate idle poll traffic versus write-driven traffic.
Count replicas and multiply by per-replica buffer memory.
Set `client-output-buffer-limit` per replica class.
Reassess the model when replica count grows past a few dozen.

redis-replication--curated-4.how: The master inspects each replica's output buffer and disconnects one that exceeds `client-output-buffer-limit` or stops responding within `repl-timeout`. The replica must then resync from scratch.
steps: Set a hard output-buffer limit per replica.
Alert before the limit is reached, not after.
Investigate replicas that repeatedly disconnect.
Keep a spare replica path so a resync does not stall failover.

redis-replication--curated-5.how: Set `min-replicas-to-write` with `min-replicas-max-lag` so the master refuses writes without enough caught-up replicas, and use `WAIT` when a specific caller needs an acknowledgement from at least one replica.
steps: Decide how much acknowledged-but-unreplicated data you can lose.
Configure the minimum replica count and lag bound.
Use `WAIT` for the specific writes that need it.
Route critical reads to the master or after a `WAIT`.

redis-replication--curated-6.how: Enable `repl-diskless-sync yes` so a full resync writes the RDB directly to the replica socket instead of to disk and back. Available since Redis 2.8.18.
steps: Check your Redis version supports diskless sync.
Enable it on masters that do frequent full resyncs.
Measure master disk I/O before and after.
Watch network throughput during snapshot transfer.

cdn-content-replication.context: A distributed-systems explainer on how CDNs replicate, invalidate, and pay for content across hundreds of edge locations.

cdn-content-replication--curated-1.how: CDNs place copies near users and accept that pushes and purges land at different times on different edges. They report propagation in percentiles rather than promising an instant global switch.
steps: Decide which assets can tolerate stale reads.
Measure propagation time for your provider's purge and push.
Design deploys so mixed versions can coexist.
Reserve strong consistency for data that truly needs it.

cdn-content-replication--curated-2.how: A push job becomes a DAG from origin to tier-1 parents, then mid-tier caches, then edges, with chunked parallel transfers. On reads, request coalescing lets one miss go upstream while the rest wait on that result.
steps: Keep the origin out of direct fan-out to every edge.
Enable request collapsing at each cache tier.
Chunk large files for parallel internal transfer.
Warm parent tiers before a scheduled release.

cdn-content-replication--curated-3.how: Assign each content class a strategy: push for large, stable, or time-critical objects; pull for the long tail; and let traffic analysis promote objects that suddenly get hot.
steps: Classify assets by size, change rate, and audience spread.
Push firmware, bundles, and event streams.
Leave rarely requested assets to pull.
Configure rules that promote or evict by request rate.

cdn-content-replication--curated-4.how: Compute a hash of the bytes and put it in the filename or query string so it becomes part of the cache key. Serve an ETag and honor `If-None-Match` with a 304 to skip unchanged payloads.
steps: Add a content hash to every static asset URL.
Set long cache lifetimes on hashed assets.
Keep unhashed HTML on a short TTL.
Send ETag and support conditional requests.

cdn-content-replication--curated-5.how: Track propagation percentiles and avoid purge-driven invalidation where possible. Use short TTLs plus `stale-while-revalidate` so edges serve the old copy while one request refreshes it.
steps: Log time from purge to last edge updated.
Prefer TTL expiry over purge for frequently changing assets.
Add `stale-while-revalidate` to cache headers.
Rate-limit or collapse refreshes after an invalidation.

cdn-content-replication--curated-6.how: Model cost per object as storage multiplied by edge count, plus origin egress for pushes and for every miss that reaches back. Replicate only content whose demand justifies the copies.
steps: Estimate storage cost per asset across all edges.
Track origin egress from both pushes and misses.
Set cache rules that exclude long-tail content from broad replication.
Review cost per asset class quarterly.

grpc-http2.context: An explainer on why gRPC was built on HTTP/2 and what that choice changes for streaming, metadata, and mesh operations.

grpc-http2--curated-1.how: gRPC maps each call to an HTTP/2 stream and carries serialized protobuf messages in DATA frames, so unary and all three streaming shapes share one transport without upgrades or separate protocols.
steps: List which of your calls actually need streaming.
Use bidirectional streams where both sides push independently.
Avoid layering custom streaming over unary calls.
Verify your proxies preserve stream semantics.

grpc-http2--curated-2.how: Each call gets a stream ID and frames from different streams interleave on one connection. A slow response occupies its own stream rather than the whole socket.
steps: Consolidate per-peer connection pools into one or two HTTP/2 connections.
Confirm your client library multiplexes by default.
Test with one deliberately slow dependency in the call chain.
Watch for head-of-line blocking reintroduced by TCP-level issues.

grpc-http2--curated-3.how: Model connections as services times peers times connections per peer: six each gives 540 in a ten-service mesh, one or two gives 180. Measure latency and requests per second before and after consolidating.
steps: Inventory current connection counts per service pair.
Reduce pool size per peer to one or two HTTP/2 connections.
Load test concurrent fan-out calls.
Compare p99 latency and throughput against the old setup.

grpc-http2--curated-4.how: HTTP/2 keeps a dynamic header table and sends an index for values already seen, so repeated auth, tracing, and content-type headers cost a few bytes per call instead of full text.
steps: Audit which headers every hop forwards.
Drop headers that do not need to propagate.
Keep header values stable so HPACK can index them.
Measure per-call metadata size in a service mesh trace.

grpc-http2--curated-5.how: Each stream starts with a 65 KB flow-control window. The receiver issues `WINDOW_UPDATE` as it consumes bytes, and the sender cannot exceed the unacknowledged window.
steps: Leave flow control enabled on streaming calls.
Tune initial window size for high-latency links.
Make consumers acknowledge as they process.
Alert when a stream stalls on a zero window.

grpc-http2--curated-6.how: Match the protocol to the workload: HTTP/1.1 for one-off calls from constrained clients, HTTP/2 where concurrency or streaming dominates. Check that every load balancer in the path handles HTTP/2 and trailers natively.
steps: Measure whether your traffic is concurrent or single-shot.
Confirm load balancers pass HTTP/2 end to end.
Budget memory for HPACK and stream state on small devices.
Keep HTTP/1.1 fallback for simple clients.

why-consensus.context: A conceptual piece that precedes a Raft deep dive, explaining why agreement across replicas is required and what consensus guarantees.

why-consensus--curated-1.how: Consensus protocols elect a leader through a majority and replicate an ordered log, so every non-faulty node applies the same operations in the same sequence despite failures.
steps: List the state that more than one node can mutate.
Decide which parts need a single agreed order.
Use an existing consensus-backed store for that state.
Keep data that tolerates stale reads out of the consensus path.

why-consensus--curated-2.how: The three-replica example applies withdrawals locally with no shared ordering: $1,000 minus $800 on one node, minus $500 on another, and a third sees a different sequence. The balance diverges even though each local computation is valid.
steps: Find operations that read a value and write a derived one.
Route them through a single ordered path or a conditional write.
Add a test that issues conflicting writes to two replicas.
Verify the final state matches one serial order.

why-consensus--curated-3.how: State safety as an invariant that must never be violated and liveness as a progress condition that must eventually hold; test them separately with partitions and with node restarts.
steps: Write the safety invariant for each replicated decision.
Write the liveness expectation with a time bound.
Fault-inject partitions and check safety holds.
Fault-inject failures and check progress resumes.

why-consensus--curated-4.how: Require a majority for election and writes: three of five nodes can act, two cannot. The minority detects lost quorum and fails closed instead of diverging.
steps: Use an odd cluster size so majorities are unambiguous.
Gate writes and elections on quorum.
Make the minority side reject writes.
Test a symmetric partition and confirm one side stops.

why-consensus--curated-5.how: Recognize consensus where it already runs: primary election in replicated databases, two-phase commit across shards, Kafka's controller, service registries, config rollout, and etcd for Kubernetes state.
steps: Map each subsystem that stores cluster state.
Identify where it gets its agreed order from.
Avoid building a second source of truth beside it.
Read that system's failure behavior before relying on it.

database-deadlocks.context: A production-oriented explainer on why database deadlocks happen, how engines detect and resolve them, and how to prevent them.

database-deadlocks--curated-1.how: Treat deadlock handling as three layers: prevent cycles with a global lock order, let the engine detect what remains through its wait-for graph, and retry transactions that get aborted.
steps: Document the lock order for every multi-row write path.
Keep transactions short so cycles have less time to form.
Add retry logic at the transaction boundary.
Track deadlock rate as a service metric.

database-deadlocks--curated-2.how: The engine periodically builds a directed graph of transactions waiting on each other, searches for a cycle, and aborts a chosen victim. PostgreSQL checks after `deadlock_timeout`; SQL Server every five seconds.
steps: Learn your engine's detection interval.
Read the deadlock log to see the cycle it found.
Identify which transaction was aborted and why.
Make the application tolerate that abort with a retry.

database-deadlocks--curated-3.how: Audit for the four hidden sources: plan changes on similar statements, lock escalation from rows to tables, foreign-key checks on child rows, and long transactions that hold everything longer.
steps: Compare execution plans for statements that touch the same tables.
Watch for lock escalation in engine metrics.
Account for foreign-key locks in write ordering.
Split long transactions into shorter ones.

database-deadlocks--curated-4.how: PostgreSQL's `deadlock_timeout` defaults to one second and trades detection delay for low overhead; MySQL detects simple cycles immediately and falls back to timeout-based resolution for complex ones via `innodb_lock_wait_timeout`.
steps: Check your engine's default detection behavior.
Lower the timeout only if waits are genuinely short.
Measure CPU cost before shortening detection intervals.
Align application retry timing with the detection delay.

database-deadlocks--curated-5.how: Enforce one acquisition order in code, keep transactions brief, and retry from the start when the engine reports a deadlock, because the whole transaction was rolled back.
steps: Sort resources by a stable key before locking.
Move non-database work outside the transaction.
Retry the full transaction with backoff and jitter.
Cap retries so a persistent cycle fails fast.

database-deadlocks--curated-6.how: Turn on deadlock logging, keep the statement pairs, and correlate with slow query logs, since statements that wait on locks are the ones most likely to be involved in a cycle.

cpu-cache-locality.context: Part of a series on performance fundamentals, explaining the CPU cache hierarchy and how memory access patterns change real-world speed.

cpu-cache-locality--curated-1.how: Measure wall-clock time for the same algorithm under different memory layouts; the essay reports 10x to 100x differences from access order alone.
steps: Pick a hot loop over a large data structure.
Time it, then time a version that walks memory sequentially.
Compare the gap against the operation count.
Treat layout as a first-class performance decision.

cpu-cache-locality--curated-2.how: The hierarchy is documented per level: registers ~1 cycle, L1 1-3 cycles at 32-64 KB, L2 10-20 cycles, L3 40-75 cycles shared, RAM 200-300 cycles.
steps: Estimate the working set of your hot path.
Compare it with L1, L2 and L3 capacities.
If it spills past L3, expect memory-bound behaviour.
Shrink or block the working set before optimising instructions.

cpu-cache-locality--curated-3.how: Separate the two effects by asking whether a loop revisits the same address or merely walks adjacent ones; the fixes differ.
steps: Identify whether the hot loop reuses addresses or streams through them.
For reuse, keep data resident and avoid re-allocation.
For streaming, make the access order sequential.
Do not expect a reuse fix to help a streaming workload.

cpu-cache-locality--curated-4.how: Benchmark an n-by-n matrix initialisation in row-major and column-major order across increasing sizes; the gap grows once the matrix exceeds cache.
steps: Write the same matrix fill both ways.
Run at sizes that fit in cache and sizes that do not.
Compare runtimes, not operation counts.
Reorder loops so the innermost index matches memory layout.

cpu-cache-locality--curated-5.how: Redis samples keys into a static array of about 16 eviction candidates, sorted by idle time or access frequency, so the whole pool fits in a few cache lines.
steps: Find a latency-critical structure that is currently a linked list.
Check whether its size is bounded and small.
Move it into a contiguous array or fixed-size pool.
Measure the reduction in cache misses on that path.

cpu-cache-locality--curated-6.how: Compare asymptotic cost with measured cache behaviour; the essay notes a linear scan can beat a logarithmic search at realistic sizes.
steps: Profile cache miss rate and instructions per cycle with `perf`.
Benchmark the asymptotically better algorithm on real data.
Check whether its access pattern is scattered.
Choose the version that wins on measured time, not Big O alone.

eventual-consistency.context: One of a series of posts on distributed-systems consistency models, framed around CAP and production examples such as DynamoDB, DNS and social feeds.

eventual-consistency--curated-1.how: Compare the cost of a write that waits for all replicas with one that is acknowledged locally and replicated asynchronously.
steps: Map which operations cross a region boundary.
Measure the round-trip latency to the farthest replica.
Decide per operation whether a write may return early.
Document the staleness window users can tolerate.

eventual-consistency--curated-2.how: The essay walks a three-region profile update: wait for New York, London and Tokyo, or acknowledge in Tokyo and propagate.
steps: List the partitions your system must survive.
Accept that partition tolerance cannot be dropped.
For each write path, choose refuse-on-partition or accept-and-merge.
Keep the choice explicit in the service contract.

eventual-consistency--curated-3.how: Define the guarantee precisely: replicas converge once updates stop, with no promised upper bound on the delay.
steps: Classify each read as needing fresh or tolerant data.
Route tolerant reads to local replicas.
Route sensitive reads through a stronger path.
Tell users what delay to expect rather than implying instant consistency.

eventual-consistency--curated-4.how: Strong consistency requires an acknowledgement per replica, so latency tracks the slowest path and throughput tracks coordination overhead.
steps: Count how many replicas each write must reach.
Estimate throughput lost to waiting.
Compare with local-write plus background sync.
Keep strong coordination only for writes that need it.

eventual-consistency--curated-5.how: Read-your-writes is implemented by pinning a user's reads to their own replica or session, while vector clocks and CRDTs handle concurrent merges.
steps: Give authors an immediate read of their own write.
Let other readers tolerate a short delay.
Use vector clocks to order concurrent updates.
Use CRDTs where merges must be automatic.

eventual-consistency--curated-6.how: Draw the boundary at operations where a stale read creates a real loss: transfers, balances and audit records.
steps: List operations where double spending is possible.
Require strong consistency for balance checks and transfers.
Keep eventual consistency for profiles, feeds and counters.
Test the failure path with a partitioned replica.

eventual-consistency--curated-7.how: The essay suggests a deliberate delay in the interface, such as a five-second publish animation, to cover replication lag.
steps: Find user actions that feel incomplete without confirmation.
Add honest progress feedback that covers the replication window.
Avoid promising that other users already see the change.
Measure whether the delay actually hides the lag.

dns-udp-tcp.context: Part of a series on internet infrastructure that goes past the common shorthand that DNS only uses UDP.

dns-udp-tcp--curated-1.how: Trace a real lookup end to end and note which transport each hop uses; UDP for ordinary queries, TCP for truncated answers and zone transfers.
steps: Capture traffic for a normal lookup and a DNSSEC-signed one.
Identify which responses arrive over UDP and which over TCP.
Check that both are permitted on port 53.
Document the branch in your runbooks.

dns-udp-tcp--curated-2.how: Compare packet counts: two for a UDP exchange versus at least seven for TCP once handshake and teardown are counted.
steps: Measure query volume per second on your resolver.
Estimate the connection table TCP would require.
Keep UDP as the default path.
Reserve TCP for answers that do not fit.

dns-udp-tcp--curated-3.how: The server sets TC in the response header when the answer exceeds the advertised UDP size; the resolver retries the same query over TCP.
steps: Advertise an EDNS0 buffer size in the query.
Check the TC bit on every response.
On truncation or timeout, retry the identical query over TCP.
Cache the result so the retry is not repeated.

dns-udp-tcp--curated-4.how: The essay lists the size drivers: DNSSEC signatures, long SPF/DKIM TXT records, many A/AAAA answers, CNAME chains, and AXFR/IXFR transfers that are TCP-only.
steps: Audit your zones for DNSSEC and long TXT records.
Check how many addresses or aliases a typical answer returns.
Test resolution through a middlebox that limits UDP size.
Confirm zone transfers use TCP by design.

dns-udp-tcp--curated-5.how: Resolvers record that a name or query type needs TCP and use that knowledge on the next lookup, or issue UDP and TCP in parallel for critical names.
steps: Measure how often fallback happens per name.
Cache the protocol requirement alongside the answer.
Prefer direct TCP for known-large records.
Consider parallel queries only for latency-critical paths.

dns-udp-tcp--curated-6.how: Check firewall, load-balancer and monitoring configuration for port 53 on both protocols, then watch the fallback rate as the leading indicator.
steps: Open UDP and TCP 53 everywhere DNS must pass.
Verify load balancers forward both.
Track UDP success rate and TCP fallback frequency.
Alert on response-size and timeout anomalies.

okr.context: A practical guide to writing OKRs, based on the author's use of the framework at engineering organisations and for personal planning since 2020.

okr--curated-1.how: Test each key result by asking whether it can reach completion while the objective remains unmet; if so, it measures activity.
steps: Take your current key results.
Ask what number each one moves.
Rewrite any that only describe completed work.
Check that the set covers the objective, not just the backlog.

okr--curated-2.how: The guide caps a cycle at two to three objectives, each with two to four measurable key results.
steps: List every candidate objective for the quarter.
Rank by business impact.
Keep two or three and park the rest.
Give each survivor no more than four key results.

okr--curated-3.how: Replace "test and deploy the Payments Batch API" with the outcome the deployment should produce, moving the testing detail into the description.
steps: Find key results that start with a verb like ship, build or migrate.
Ask what changes for the business once it is done.
State that change as the key result.
Move the task detail into the description or an issue.

okr--curated-4.how: The guide contrasts "improve API performance" with a version that names the metric and the target it must reach.
steps: Highlight every key result containing improve, enhance or optimise.
Name the specific metric behind the verb.
Record the current value and the target value.
Confirm the metric is not the easiest one to move.

okr--curated-5.how: Compare the OKR list against the JIRA board; heavy overlap means the framework is being used as a status report.
steps: Export the quarter's epics and tickets.
Compare them with the key results.
Remove key results that are just tickets.
Restate the remainder as end-of-quarter outcomes.

okr--curated-6.how: Map engineering OKRs to product OKRs one-to-one on business outcomes, allowing separate entries only for tech debt, engineering excellence and product research.
steps: Put the engineering and product OKRs side by side.
Draw a line from each engineering result to a business outcome.
Keep separate entries only for debt and discovery.
Escalate any result with no business counterpart.

okr--curated-7.how: Run the guide's checks on each draft before committing the quarter: labels, inspiring objective, measurable results, no activities, small count, business trace.
steps: Label every objective and key result.
Rewrite the objective as a destination worth pursuing.
Attach a metric and target to each key result.
Remove task-shaped results.
Trim to two or three objectives.

theta-sketches.context: A deep dive on Theta sketches and the Apache DataSketches ecosystem, including production use at Yahoo and LinkedIn and native support in Druid and Pinot.

theta-sketches--curated-1.how: Theta sketches generalise KMV by exposing the sampling threshold, so union, intersection and difference all return a sketch that can feed the next operation.
steps: List the set questions your analytics actually asks.
If any need overlap or exclusion, rule out HLL.
Evaluate Theta sketches for those columns.
Keep HLL where only distinct counts are needed.

theta-sketches--curated-2.how: A sketch is `(theta, S)`; it starts at theta 1.0 in exact mode and lowers theta to the (k+1)-th smallest hash once |S| exceeds k.
steps: Store theta alongside the retained hashes.
Estimate cardinality as |S| divided by theta.
Let theta drop as the set grows past k.
Do not switch modes in application code.

theta-sketches--curated-3.how: Solve k from RSE = 1/sqrt(k-1), round up to a power of two, and budget 8 bytes per retained entry.
steps: Pick the relative error your query can tolerate.
Compute k from the RSE formula.
Round up to the nearest power of two.
Multiply k by 8 bytes and the number of stored sketches.

theta-sketches--curated-4.how: Take min(theta) across inputs, filter each retained set to it, then apply union, intersection or difference on the hashes.
steps: Use one hash function and seed everywhere.
Compute the minimum theta across inputs.
Drop entries at or above that theta.
Combine the remaining hashes for the operation.
Estimate the result as size divided by theta.

theta-sketches--curated-5.how: Intersection error grows as sqrt(F), where F is union cardinality divided by intersection cardinality; the essay's two-million-by-one-thousand example reaches about 71%.
steps: Estimate the expected intersection size before querying.
Compute F against the union size.
Read upper and lower bounds, not just the point estimate.
Increase k or pre-filter when F is large.

theta-sketches--curated-6.how: DataSketches validates seeds at operation time and throws on a mismatch, but stored sketches cannot be migrated to a new seed.
steps: Pick one seed for the whole pipeline.
Propagate it to every producer and merger.
Record the seed alongside stored sketches.
Treat a seed change as a full rebuild, not a config tweak.

theta-sketches--curated-7.how: Compare storage: HLL is 2-16x smaller than Theta at equal accuracy, CPC is another 30-40% smaller than HLL, and a 16384-entry Theta sketch is about 30x an lgK=12 HLL.
steps: List the query types each sketch column serves.
Use Theta only where intersection or difference is required.
Use HLL or CPC for distinct-count-only columns.
Revisit the choice when query patterns change.

3p.context: A short career-planning note describing the author's personal framework for deciding when to change jobs.

3p--curated-1.how: Score the current role on pay, competency growth and ladder growth, then count how many are genuinely being served.
steps: Rate each P honestly for the current role.
Count the ones that are actually strong.
Stay if two or more hold.
Start looking if fewer than two do.

3p--curated-2.how: Judge Power by the skills and domain depth gained, not by title, team size or scope.
steps: List what you can do now that you could not a year ago.
Check whether the work is getting harder in a useful direction.
Separate a bigger scope from deeper competence.
Treat prestige without learning as a warning sign.

3p--curated-3.how: The essay applies this to pay explicitly: a below-average salary can be worth it when the other two Ps outweigh it.
steps: Name the P that is currently weak.
Write down what the other two are providing.
Decide whether that compensation is enough.
Revisit the trade at the next review.

3p--curated-4.how: The author reviewed his situation every six months and named the two Ps he was optimising for at each employer.
steps: Put a recurring six-month review on the calendar.
Compare pay with market rate.
List new competencies from the period.
Check the promotion path.
Name the two Ps you are optimising and the one you are trading away.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.context: Notes on the AWS Lambda paper covering how the platform loads large container images on demand while preserving cold-start latency and deduplication.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.how: Lambda executes as soon as the first required blocks are resident, fetching the remainder asynchronously while the function runs.
steps: Identify what your workload needs at startup.
Separate that from what it needs only later.
Load the critical portion synchronously.
Stream the rest in the background.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.how: Images are flattened into one ext4 filesystem; a local agent serves reads from local cache, regional cache, then S3, with page-level copy-on-write for guest writes.
steps: Flatten layers deterministically before storing.
Serve reads block by block through a local agent.
Check local, then regional, then object storage.
Use copy-on-write so shared blocks stay immutable.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.how: Chunk key is the SHA-256 digest, encryption is AES-CTR with a deterministic IV, and only the manifest key table uses a per-customer KMS key.
steps: Hash each chunk to derive its key.
Encrypt with a deterministic IV.
Keep offsets, keys and hashes in a manifest.
Encrypt the manifest key table per customer.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.how: Production telemetry over newly uploaded functions: 80% had zero unique chunks, the rest averaged 4.3% unique with a 2.5% median.
steps: Measure unique bytes per new deployment.
Compare against shared base layers.
Estimate transfer saved by block-level loading.
Use the ratio to justify a dedupe layer.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.how: Key derivation includes a salt that can rotate by time, chunk popularity or placement, limiting how many images depend on one chunk.
steps: Identify chunks shared across tenants.
Add a rotatable salt to key derivation.
Choose the rotation axis: time, popularity or placement.
Measure the dedupe ratio lost against the exposure reduced.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.how: The production deployment uses a 4-of-5 erasure code: any four of five chunks reconstruct the data, at 25% storage overhead and 25% more requests.
steps: Split data into fixed-size chunks.
Encode with a 4-of-5 scheme.
Store the encoded pieces instead of replicas.
Serve from any four to route around slow shards.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.context: Notes on the GoogleSQL paper that proposes pipe syntax as an extension to standard SQL for more readable, composable queries.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.how: Pipe syntax lets a query start at FROM and continue with `|>` stages, so the written order matches the execution order.
steps: Take a nested query and list its stages in execution order.
Rewrite it as a linear chain of stages.
Remove duplicate WHERE, HAVING and QUALIFY workarounds.
Check that each stage reads top to bottom.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.how: Each operator maps one input table to one output table and sees only its arguments, which is the contract that permits arbitrary composition.
steps: Model each step as a table in, table out transform.
Keep arguments local to the stage.
Reorder stages to test composability.
Reuse a stage more than once in a pipeline.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.how: Any prefix of a pipeline is still a valid query, which the paper calls the prefix property and uses for debugging operators.
steps: Run the query up to the stage before the suspected bug.
Inspect the intermediate table.
Attach `LOG` to see rows and `DESCRIBE` to see the schema.
Use `ASSERT` to fail on an invalid intermediate state.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.how: `CALL` invokes table-valued functions as a stage, and `PIVOT` is expressed as an ordinary pipe operator rather than a special clause.
steps: Replace a nested TVF subquery with a `CALL` stage.
Express pivots as a pipeline step.
Keep joins and aggregations in piped form.
Add new operators without new reserved keywords.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.how: GoogleSQL made pipes a suffix on existing queries and reused one language-analysis component across F1, BigQuery, Spanner and Procella.
steps: Keep existing SQL valid during rollout.
Convert one stage per query rather than rewriting all at once.
Confirm the engine produces the same algebra.
Share the parser across engines instead of forking.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.context: Notes on the NanoLog paper describing a logging system optimised for nanosecond-scale overhead in latency-sensitive applications.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.how: NanoLog splits logging into compile-time code generation, a lock-free runtime record step, and post-execution formatting by a background thread.
steps: Measure what your logger costs per call today.
Identify formatting, locking and I/O on the hot path.
Move static work to compile time.
Move formatting and persistence off the calling thread.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.how: The preprocessor parses each format string, infers argument types and emits a `record()` for dynamic values and a `compact()` for compression, keyed by a compile-time log id.
steps: Parse the format string at build time.
Generate type-specific capture code per statement.
Assign each statement a stable id.
Store file, line, severity and format in a dictionary.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.how: Each logging thread gets a fixed-size single-producer, single-consumer circular queue; appends are atomic and an emission thread drains it.
steps: Give every logging thread its own buffer.
Make it a fixed-size ring with one producer and one consumer.
Append atomically without locks.
Drain asynchronously on a background thread.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.how: Private fields for the logging and background threads are aligned to cache-line boundaries using `__attribute__((aligned(CACHE_LINE_SIZE)))`.
steps: Find fields written by different threads on the same line.
Pad or align them to 64-byte boundaries.
Re-measure throughput under contention.
Accept the small memory cost for the coherence win.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.how: Each integer is stored in the minimum bytes needed, prefixed with a 4-bit header for length and sign, so small values take about 1.5 bytes.
steps: Check the value distribution of your logged integers.
Encode each in the fewest bytes possible.
Prefix a nibble recording length and sign.
Avoid general-purpose compression on the hot path.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.how: Parameters are written as binary values with a time-stamp-counter timestamp; a decompressor joins them with the dictionary to rebuild text later.
steps: Log binary values instead of formatted strings.
Use a cheap clock source mapped to wall time.
Store the static format once in a dictionary.
Render text offline during decompression.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.context: Notes on Twitter's Who to Follow paper, part of a series of paper notes on large-scale distributed systems. It covers the recommendation service's in-memory graph engine and its later distributed rewrite.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.how: The first-generation service loaded the full follower graph into Cassovary on one host, so recommendation queries touched RAM instead of disk or remote partitions. The second generation partitioned the graph across servers and added redundancy and failover.
steps: Measure the working set your hottest query needs.
If it fits in one machine's memory, prototype the centralized version first.
Track memory growth against hardware limits.
Define the threshold that triggers a distributed rewrite before you hit it.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.how: Count the graph hops one recommendation needs, then compare RAM access time with the disk or RPC latency in your stack. The gap determines whether the algorithm can run synchronously.
steps: Count graph reads per recommendation.
Measure the latency of each read path.
Multiply to get the per-request I/O budget.
Move the graph into memory if I/O dominates the budget.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.how: Run many short walks from the query user, count how often each node is visited, and rank candidates by visit frequency. The essay describes this as the local half of the recommender.
steps: Choose a walk length that stays within a few hops.
Run enough walks for stable visit counts.
Aggregate visits per candidate node.
Drop the query user and already-followed accounts.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.how: Model users and content as two node sets, alternate score updates between them, and blend the resulting authority scores with walk-based proximity when ranking follows.
steps: Build the user-content bipartite view.
Iterate scores across both sides until stable.
Keep authority as a separate signal from proximity.
Blend the two rankings and test the mix.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.how: Watch memory headroom and recovery time as leading indicators. When either approaches its limit, move to a partitioned graph with replicas rather than repeatedly buying a bigger host.
steps: Track memory headroom per quarter.
Measure time to rebuild the graph after a crash.
Set triggers for a partitioned redesign.
Keep the old path available during migration.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.how: Lay out the graph around traversal: contiguous adjacency arrays, fixed-width node IDs and minimal per-node metadata. Benchmark bytes per edge before adding convenience fields.
steps: Measure bytes per node and per edge.
Store neighbours in contiguous arrays.
Use fixed-width identifiers.
Audit optional fields that inflate every node.

structure-your-design-interviews.context: A short guide to running a 40-45 minute system design interview, based on the author's own interview routine.

structure-your-design-interviews--curate.how: Write the five phase budgets on a sheet before the interview and check the clock at each boundary, adjusting only the depth of the later phases.
steps: Decide phase budgets before the call.
State the plan to the interviewer.
Check the clock at each phase boundary.
Protect time for follow-up discussion.

structure-your-design-interviews--curate.how: Ask about users, read/write mix, scale, latency targets, consistency needs and existing infrastructure, then restate the problem in one sentence for confirmation.
steps: Ask who uses the system and at what scale.
Confirm read and write proportions.
Ask which qualities matter most.
Restate the problem and get agreement.

structure-your-design-interviews--curate.how: Sketch the minimum end-to-end path in five to seven minutes and explicitly label what you are deferring.
steps: Sketch clients, API, service and store.
Trace one read and one write.
Name the parts you are deferring.
Ask whether the direction is right.

structure-your-design-interviews--curate.how: Keep the phase lengths visible and negotiate small shifts with the interviewer rather than silently overrunning.

keep-yourself-unblocked.context: A career-growth essay on how the author gets unstuck at work, written for software engineers who report progress in standups.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-1.how: Set a time limit on solo attempts, then move through the unblocking options in order instead of waiting for inspiration.
steps: Set a hard time-box for solo debugging.
Name the specific unknown blocking you.
Pick the next unblocking route.
Record what finally worked.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-2.how: Decide in advance how long you will try alone, then climb one rung at a time rather than jumping straight to escalation.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-3.how: Explain the goal, what you expected, what happened and what you already ruled out. Ask the listener to repeat the story back before they suggest anything.
steps: State the intended behaviour.
State the observed behaviour.
List what you have ruled out.
Ask for a restatement before advice.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-4.how: Pick a bounded task that takes ten to twenty minutes, finish it, then return to the block with a written note of where you stopped.
steps: Write down the current state and next question.
Choose a bounded unrelated task.
Finish that task completely.
Return and reread your note.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-5.how: List the unknowns, pick the one that blocks the most others, and design the smallest experiment that resolves it.
steps: List every unknown in the block.
Rank them by what they unblock.
Pick the smallest testable one.
Resolve it before expanding scope.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-6.how: Bring the other team the specific ask, the deadline and the impact of delay. If the queue does not move, escalate with that same context rather than a complaint.
steps: Identify the owning team and the exact ask.
Explain the deadline and downstream impact.
Ask for an explicit priority decision.
Escalate with written context if it stalls.

keep-yourself-unblocked--curated-7.how: Give the model the error, the relevant code and what you tried, ask for candidate causes, then test each one against the system.
steps: Paste the error and the smallest repro.
Ask for several candidate causes.
Rank them by how cheaply you can test.
Confirm the real cause before changing code.

genetic-knapsack.context: Part of a series on algorithms and data structures. This essay builds a genetic algorithm for 0/1 knapsack on a four-item example and measures how close it gets.

genetic-knapsack--curated-1.how: Use the exact DP when capacity is small; switch to a genetic algorithm when capacity is huge and a near-optimal pack is acceptable.
steps: Estimate the exact DP's runtime from n and W.
Decide whether near-optimal is acceptable.
If so, budget population and generations.
Report the best individual and its gap.

genetic-knapsack--curated-2.how: Express runtime in terms of input length, not numeric magnitude: if the bound contains the value of a number rather than its bit length, treat it as exponential.
steps: Find numeric parameters in the complexity.
Ask how many bits each needs.
Rewrite the bound in terms of bit length.
Flag any algorithm with a value in the exponent.

genetic-knapsack--curated-3.how: Map one gene to one item, compute weight and value in a single pass, and return zero for any overweight candidate rather than a scaled-down score.
steps: Map each gene to one decision.
Compute weight and value in one pass.
Return zero for infeasible candidates.
Verify fitness against a brute-force check.

genetic-knapsack--curated-4.how: Selection runs a pairwise tournament per parent slot, then every child passes through crossover, mutation or reproduction according to the configured rates. For larger problems the essay suggests populations between 500 and 50,000 and notes that two-point crossover converged fastest.
steps: Sample two candidates uniformly.
Keep the higher-fitness one.
Repeat for the second parent.
Apply crossover, mutation or reproduction by rate.

genetic-knapsack--curated-5.how: Log best and average fitness per generation, cap the run at 500 generations, and stop early after 50 generations without improvement.
steps: Log best and average fitness each generation.
Plot both to see the plateau.
Cap generations up front.
Stop after 50 flat generations.

genetic-knapsack--curated-6.how: Benchmark one fitness evaluation, multiply by the population and generation caps, and check the estimate against the latency budget.
steps: Benchmark one fitness evaluation.
Choose population and generation caps.
Multiply to estimate total work.
Tune parameters against that budget.

genetic-knapsack--curated-7.how: Write down the objective, hand-score several known candidates, and compare the fitness function's ranking with your own before scaling up.
steps: State the objective in one sentence.
Hand-score several known candidates.
Compare the function's ranking to yours.
Add missing constraints before scaling up.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr.context: Part of a series on pseudorandom number generation, following an essay on Rule 30 cellular automata. This one implements an LFSR in Go and uses it to scramble bytes.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr--cur.how: Choose n, a non-zero seed and a tap set, then step the register once per output bit and reconstruct state from the same configuration whenever you need to replay.
steps: Pick a register width for the cycle you need.
Choose a non-zero seed.
Select taps for a maximal period.
Store the configuration with any generated data.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr--cur.how: Implement `NextBit` as: read the low bit, XOR it with the tap bits, shift right, then OR the feedback into the high bit.
steps: Read the output bit.
XOR it with each tap bit.
Shift the register right.
Write the feedback into the top bit.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr--cur.how: Prefer known maximal-length tap sets for the chosen width, verify the period empirically, and reject any configuration that repeats inside the expected run.
steps: Pick taps from a maximal-length table.
Run until the seed recurs.
Record the period.
Reject periods shorter than the workload.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr--cur.how: Loop k times, shift the accumulator left, OR in the next bit, and return the result; the register state carries across calls.
steps: Decide the output width.
Shift the accumulator left.
Insert the next bit.
Repeat for k bits.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr--cur.how: Initialize the LFSR from the shared configuration, generate one 8-bit number per input byte, and XOR in order; decrypt by replaying the identical sequence.
steps: Share n, seed and taps.
Generate one byte per input byte.
XOR in stream order.
Replay identically to reverse.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr--cur.how: Treat any LFSR used for masking or scrambling as obfuscation only; for secrets, use a cryptographic generator instead.
steps: Classify whether the data is secret.
If yes, reject LFSR.
Use a cryptographic PRNG.
Keep LFSR for counters and noise.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.context: Part of a series on distributed data storage, following an essay on range- and hash-based partitioning. It uses a partitioned `movies` collection as the running example.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.how: List the top queries first, mark which include the partition key, then choose local indexes for partition-bound queries and global indexes for the rest.
steps: List the production query patterns.
Mark which filter on the partition key.
Map each query to one partition or many.
Choose an index type per query.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.how: Store index entries as attribute value plus primary key, and resolve the record with a second lookup against the owning partition.
steps: Choose the attribute to index.
Store value plus record key.
Resolve records by key.
Track index size separately.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.how: Create the index inside each partition's storage engine and route queries by partition key before consulting it.
steps: Confirm queries carry the partition key.
Build the index per partition.
Update base and index together.
Reject queries that lack the key.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.how: Detect queries that filter only on the indexed attribute, and either route them to a global index or accept and bound the fan-out.
steps: Find queries without the partition key.
Count partitions each would hit.
Measure fan-out latency.
Route them to a global index.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.how: Build a separate index table keyed by the indexed attribute, partitioned independently, and point queries at it instead of the base partitions.
steps: Pick the attribute to partition by.
Build a separate index table.
Route global queries there.
Keep record IDs for the fetch.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.how: Decide per index whether reads can tolerate staleness. If yes, update asynchronously and document the lag; if no, budget for synchronous cross-partition writes.
steps: Ask whether stale reads are acceptable.
If yes, update asynchronously.
Measure and publish the lag.
If no, cost the distributed write.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.context: Part of a series on distributed data storage. This essay compares range-based and hash-based horizontal partitioning and the workloads where each breaks.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.how: Estimate per-partition request volume from real access logs before choosing boundaries, and rebalance when one partition's share drifts.
steps: Collect per-key request counts.
Group keys by traffic.
Draw boundaries with equal load.
Recheck after growth.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.how: Define explicit boundaries per partition, keep a small routing table of ranges, and binary-search it for the owner.
steps: Sort the key space.
Assign contiguous ranges.
Store the boundary table.
Route with a binary search.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.how: Test the scheme against the write pattern, not the data volume: if writes always target the newest range, add a hash or bucket dimension.
steps: Map writes to partitions over a day.
Check whether one range dominates.
Add a hash prefix if it does.
Keep time as a secondary sort.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.how: Use a fast non-cryptographic hash, map hash ranges to nodes, and use consistent hashing when nodes join or leave.
steps: Choose a stable hash function.
Map hash ranges to nodes.
Route reads by rehashing.
Use consistent hashing for membership changes.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.how: Count range queries in the workload before choosing a hash. If they are common, either keep a separate ordered index or use a composite key.
steps: Count range queries in production.
Estimate partitions per scan.
Compare with a range layout.
Add an ordered index if needed.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.how: Choose a high-cardinality partition key for spread and a range key that matches the query's sort order, then keep range scans within one partition key.
steps: Pick a partition key with many values.
Pick a range key matching query order.
Keep scans under one partition key.
Watch for hot partition keys.

data-partitioning.context: The opening essay in a series on distributed data storage. It covers why databases are partitioned, how partition keys route queries, and the horizontal versus vertical split.

data-partitioning--curated-1.how: Pick an attribute present in your hottest queries, split records into disjoint segments by it, and route every request through the same mapping.
steps: Identify the attribute queries filter on.
Split records into disjoint segments.
Route requests with one mapping.
Verify each record has one owner.

data-partitioning--curated-2.how: Trace each query to its partition key. If the key is missing, either add it to the query or accept a fan-out.
steps: List queries and their filters.
Check for the partition key.
Rewrite queries to include it.
Flag the rest as fan-outs.

data-partitioning--curated-3.how: Measure rows scanned per query before and after partitioning; the reduction in working set is the latency win.
steps: Measure rows scanned today.
Estimate rows per partition.
Compare localized query latency.
Parallelize the cross-partition path.

data-partitioning--curated-4.how: Separate read and write load in your metrics. If writes saturate the master, introduce partitions with independent masters rather than more read replicas.
steps: Chart read versus write load.
Find the write bottleneck.
Split records across masters.
Keep replicas for reads only.

data-partitioning--curated-5.how: Place each partition's replicas on different failure domains and test recovery by taking one primary down.
steps: Map partitions to nodes.
Place replicas on separate hosts.
Test a primary failure.
Verify the slice is recoverable.

data-partitioning--curated-6.how: Choose horizontal for row-count and throughput growth; choose vertical when queries repeatedly read a narrow column set from wide records.
steps: Check whether growth is rows or columns.
Use horizontal for row growth.
Use vertical for wide, narrow reads.
Measure query column coverage.

leaderless-replication.context: Part of a series on replication in distributed databases. It explains quorum-based leaderless replication as an alternative to leader-centric designs.

leaderless-replication--curated-1.how: Send each write to N replicas, count acks to w, send each read to r replicas, and return the highest version among the responses.
steps: Set n, w and r.
Fan out writes and count acks.
Fan out reads and collect versions.
Return the highest version.

leaderless-replication--curated-2.how: Identify whether your write path depends on one node. If a single master outage halts writes, that is the gap a quorum design closes.
steps: Map the write path.
Find single-node dependencies.
Test a master outage.
Measure write downtime.

leaderless-replication--curated-3.how: Attach a version to every write, compare versions on read, and keep the write with the greatest version when replicas diverge.
steps: Add a version field per record.
Increment on each write.
Compare on read.
Keep the highest version.

leaderless-replication--curated-4.how: Choose an odd replica count, set w and r to a majority, and fail the operation if the ack count falls short.
steps: Use an odd number of replicas.
Write to all replicas.
Wait for a majority of acks.
Fail below the quorum.

leaderless-replication--curated-5.how: Pick w and r so their sum exceeds n, then verify the overlap arithmetic before deploying; lower either only if stale reads are acceptable.
steps: Write down n.
Choose w and r.
Check w + r > n.
Document the consistency level.

leaderless-replication--curated-6.how: Choose client fan-out for full control and few clients; choose a coordinator when many clients should not each implement quorum logic.
steps: Count the client implementations.
Assess quorum logic duplication.
Pick fan-out or coordinator.
Keep the coordinator stateless per request.

leaderless-replication--curated-7.how: On restart, exchange version summaries with peers, request anything newer, and apply the missing writes before serving reads.
steps: Compare versions with peers.
Request newer records.
Apply missing writes.
Serve reads after catch-up.

master-replica-replication.context: An overview of the Master-Replica pattern in a series on replication; it sets up the later essays on failure handling, log formats and replication strategies.

master-replica-replication--curated-1.how: Deploy N identical nodes holding the full dataset, designate one as the write master, and route reads to the other N-1 replicas.
steps: Replicate the full dataset to every node.
Route all writes to exactly one designated node.
Send reads to the other N-1 copies.
Treat the master role as an assignment, not a hardware tier.

master-replica-replication--curated-2.how: Record the commit timestamp on the master and the apply timestamp on each replica; the difference is lag. Expose it as a first-class metric and alert when it exceeds what reads can tolerate.
steps: Capture the commit time for each write.
Capture the apply time on every replica.
Expose per-replica lag as a metric.
Alert when lag exceeds the read staleness budget.

master-replica-replication--curated-3.how: Pair a failure detector with consensus-based leader election over the replicas; after a winner is chosen, reconfigure the followers and re-point clients at the new master.
steps: Detect master failure with a heartbeat or probe.
Run leader election among healthy replicas.
Promote the winner and reconfigure the followers.
Redirect clients to the new master.

master-replica-replication--curated-4.how: Compare the workload's read-to-write ratio. Replicas help only when reads dominate; when writes saturate the master, the next step is partitioning or multi-master, not more replicas.
steps: Measure the read/write ratio of the workload.
Load-test write throughput at a single master.
Check whether replicas sit idle during write bursts.
