fully-persistent-arrays.context: The second essay in a series on persistent data structures, implementing fully persistent arrays from Chuang's paper using Backer's trick from the persistent union-find literature.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-1.how: Keep one linear array as the base and represent every later version as a node in a tree of modifications, so an update allocates one node rather than a full copy.
steps: Estimate how many versions the workload will create.
Compare the memory of copy-on-write against one node per update.
Store the base array once and hang changes off it.
Measure read depth before assuming the trade is acceptable.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-2.how: Give each node `index`, `value`, and `parent` fields. Resolve a read by walking parents until one touches the requested index, then fall back to the root's cached array.
steps: Define the node with index, value, and parent.
Point the root at the initial array.
Resolve a read by walking toward the root.
Create a sibling node when branching from an old version.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-3.how: `update` allocates a node with the changed index and value and sets its parent to the version being edited; it never touches the parent's contents.
steps: Take the target version, index, and value.
Allocate a node and fill its three fields.
Point its parent at the target version.
Return the new node as the new version handle.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-4.how: Measure the average distance from the versions you read to the root. That distance is the number of parent hops each `get` performs.
steps: Instrument the number of parent hops per read.
Compare read volume with update volume.
If reads dominate, plan a rerooting step.
If writes dominate, leave the tree as is.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-5.how: Rotate the path from the old root to the chosen version so that version becomes the root, then make its materialized array the cache.
steps: Pick the version with the most reads.
Walk the path from the current root to it.
Apply rotations to make it the root.
Materialize its array as the new cache.
Repeat when the hot version changes.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-6.how: Compare the memory of m full copies against m change nodes before choosing an implementation; the naive approach is only reasonable for a handful of versions.
steps: Count expected versions and array size.
Multiply to estimate copy-on-write memory.
Compare with one node per update.
Choose the change-tree representation when versions are many.

fully-persistent-arrays--curated-7.how: Account for `create` separately: it allocates the n-slot array and the root, while later operations only allocate or traverse change nodes.
steps: Measure initialization cost against n.
Measure update cost per version.
Measure read cost as a function of depth.
Include rerooting cost if reads are hot.

persistent-data-structures-introduction.context: An introduction to persistent data structures, loosely based on the 1986 paper 'Making Data Structures Persistent' by Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator, and Tarjan, and the first essay in a series.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: Decide first which versions must be readable and which must be writable, then pick the persistence category that matches those operations.
steps: List the operations callers need on old versions.
Classify them as read-only, writable, or mergeable.
Choose partial, full, or confluent persistence accordingly.
Only then select an implementation technique.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: Map each category to the operations it permits before committing to an API; the storage technique follows from that mapping.
steps: Write down whether old versions are read-only.
Check whether old versions must accept updates.
Check whether two versions must merge.
Name the category and expose only its operations.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: On each update, copy the nodes from the root down to the changed node and share every untouched subtree with the previous version.
steps: Identify the path from root to the changed node.
Copy only the nodes on that path.
Link the copies to the existing untouched subtrees.
Keep the old root as the previous version.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: Store value-and-version entries per cell for fat nodes; cap the entries and chain overflow copies for node copying.
steps: Measure how many versions touch the hottest cell.
If the count is small, consider fat nodes.
If it can grow without bound, cap entries per node.
Chain a new copy when a node's entries are full.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: Replace whole-structure copies with path copying or node copying so an update touches only the changed path or cell.
steps: Measure update cost under naive copy-on-write.
Identify the portion that actually changes.
Copy only that path or node.
Share the rest with the previous version.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: Attach reference counting or mark-and-sweep to the version graph so nodes are freed once no live version reaches them.
steps: List which versions the application still holds.
Drop handles to versions that are no longer needed.
Use reference counting or mark-and-sweep to reclaim nodes.
Track retained-version count as a memory metric.

persistent-data-structures-introduction-.how: Look for features that need a previous state — undo stacks, historical geometry queries, immutable language runtimes — and back them with a persistent structure.
steps: Find features that reconstruct an earlier state.
Check whether the current implementation deep-copies.
Replace the copy with a persistent version handle.
Keep old handles alive only as long as the feature needs them.

constant-folding-python.context: A tour of CPython's constant-folding optimization, reading `ast_opt.c` to show how the AST is rewritten during compilation.

constant-folding-python--curated-1.how: Read `ast_opt.c`: `astfold_expr` dispatches to folders such as `fold_binop`, which call the ordinary numeric routines instead of a parallel evaluator.
steps: Open `ast_opt.c` in the CPython source.
Find `astfold_expr` and its dispatch table.
Read `fold_binop` and note which runtime functions it calls.
Confirm that folding shares semantics with normal evaluation.

constant-folding-python--curated-2.how: Use `dis.dis` on a function containing a literal arithmetic expression and look for a single `LOAD_CONST` with the computed value.
steps: Write a function returning `24 * 60 * 60`.
Run `dis.dis` on it.
Look for `LOAD_CONST 86400`.
Compare with a version using variables.

constant-folding-python--curated-3.how: Replace runtime-computed values with literals where possible; the folder can only act on operands already present in the AST.
steps: Find arithmetic on values fixed at build time.
Express those values as literals.
Disassemble to confirm folding occurred.
Leave genuinely dynamic expressions alone.

constant-folding-python--curated-4.how: Disassemble before relying on a folded constant. Check both forms, such as `2 ** 64` and `4 ** 64`, and any long string literal near the 4096 limit.
steps: List constant expressions your performance depends on.
Disassemble each one.
Replace unfolded forms with precomputed literals.
Re-check after upgrading Python.

constant-folding-python--curated-5.how: Implement an AST pass that folds children before the parent, then dispatches on node type to the general evaluation routine for that operator.
steps: Walk the AST depth-first.
Fold each operand before its parent.
Dispatch binary nodes to the matching operator function.
Write the resulting constant back into the node.

constant-folding-python--curated-6.how: Compare bytecode before and after folding to see the removed loads and operations; the benefit compounds with how often the expression executes.
steps: Disassemble the original expression.
Disassemble the literal equivalent.
Count the removed instructions.
Multiply by expected execution frequency.

string-interning-python.context: An exploration of CPython's string interning, following `PyUnicode_InternInPlace` from `unicodeobject.c` and the call sites that use it.

string-interning-python--curated-1.how: Compare two equal literals with `is` and with `==`, then inspect `PyUnicode_CHECK_INTERNED` to see how CPython records the interned state.
steps: Test equal literals with `is` and `==`.
Repeat with strings built at runtime.
Note where the results diverge.
Use identity only where interning is guaranteed.

string-interning-python--curated-2.how: Intern a string once and compare all later references against that canonical object rather than re-creating equal copies.
steps: Identify a string value used in many places.
Obtain one canonical reference.
Pass that reference instead of rebuilding the text.
Compare with `is` only on those canonical references.

string-interning-python--curated-3.how: For a hot equality check, intern both operands once, then replace the character comparison with an identity check.
steps: Profile to find repeated string equality.
Intern the strings at their boundary.
Swap `==` for `is` where both sides are canonical.
Measure the change on a realistic workload.

string-interning-python--curated-4.how: Rely on CPython's automatic interning for code-object names, dict keys, and attribute names; call `sys.intern` explicitly for other long-lived keys.
steps: Find strings used repeatedly as keys or names.
Check whether they are compile-time literals.
Use `sys.intern` for the runtime ones.
Keep interning at the boundary, not on every use.

string-interning-python--curated-5.how: Test any identity comparison against strings produced by concatenation, formatting, and input; those paths do not intern automatically.
steps: Grep for `is` comparisons between strings.
Replace them with `==` unless identity is intended.
Test with runtime-built strings.
Add a lint rule for string identity checks.

string-interning-python--curated-6.how: Call `sys.intern` on identifiers parsed from input or generated by the program before using them as dictionary keys.
steps: Find repeated keys built at runtime.
Intern each distinct key once.
Store the canonical reference.
Benchmark lookup-heavy code before and after.

string-interning-python--curated-7.how: Treat the intern table as a global cache: only intern a bounded, recurring set of strings, and never intern arbitrary user input.
steps: Estimate the distinct values that would be interned.
Reject unbounded sources such as free-text input.
Intern only known recurring identifiers.
Watch process memory as the table grows.

recursion-visualizer-python.context: A short build essay that implements a recursion visualizer as a Python decorator and publishes it as the `recviz` package.

recursion-visualizer-python--curated-1.how: Wrap the recursive function in a decorator that prints on entry and exit; the recursive body calls the rebound decorated name, so nested calls re-enter the wrapper.
steps: Write the recursive function without instrumentation.
Define a decorator that runs code before and after the call.
Apply the decorator to the function.
Confirm nested calls appear in the output.

recursion-visualizer-python--curated-2.how: Keep `recursion_level` in the enclosing scope, increment it before the wrapped call, decrement it after, and print `level * indent` spaces before each line.
steps: Declare a level counter with `nonlocal` in the wrapper.
Increment before calling the function.
Print the call line with `level * indent` spaces.
Decrement after the call returns.

recursion-visualizer-python--curated-3.how: Print `-> name(args)` before the call and `<- result` after it, preserving indentation so entry and return pair up visually.
steps: Choose distinct markers for entry and return.
Print arguments on entry.
Print the return value on exit.
Use the same indent for both lines of a call.

recursion-visualizer-python--curated-4.how: Install the published package and decorate the function rather than maintaining a local wrapper.

flajolet-martin.context: An explainer on the 1984 Flajolet-Martin probabilistic counting algorithm, with experiments on synthetic streams and the text of 'The Jungle Book'.

flajolet-martin--curated-1.how: Replace the exact set with a bit vector indexed by trailing-zero position, filled in one pass over hashed elements.
steps: Decide the acceptable error for the count.
Choose a hash range large enough for the maximum cardinality.
Allocate one bit per position.
Process the stream once and estimate from the vector.

flajolet-martin--curated-2.how: Reason from the geometric distribution: each additional trailing-zero position is half as likely, so the unseen position marks roughly log2 of the distinct count.
steps: Write down the probability for each bit position.
Relate the tail probability to the number of distinct hashes.
Find where the probability reaches zero.
Use that exponent as the estimate.

flajolet-martin--curated-3.how: For each element, hash it, find its rightmost set bit, set that bit in the vector, then take the rightmost zero position b and return 2^b.
steps: Hash each incoming element into the fixed range.
Compute the rightmost set bit position.
Set that position in the bit vector.
Scan for the rightmost zero after the stream.
Return 2 to the power of that position.

flajolet-martin--curated-4.how: Run several independent hash functions, average their estimates, and divide by 0.77351 to correct the bias.
steps: Choose multiple independent hash functions.
Maintain a bit vector per hash function.
Average the individual estimates.
Apply the 0.77351 correction.

flajolet-martin--curated-5.how: Apply a multiplicative hash with odd multipliers and a capped range so structured input is spread uniformly before trailing zeros are measured.
steps: Inspect the input for runs or ranges.
Apply a multiplicative hash with odd constants.
Cap the output range to the vector size.
Verify the positions look uniformly spread.

flajolet-martin--curated-6.how: Because the sketch only marks positions, repeated elements set the same bit as a single occurrence; no deduplication step is needed.
steps: Feed the stream without deduplicating.
Confirm repeats do not change the vector.
Compare estimates for the same set with different repetition rates.
Use the sketch where duplicates are common.

flajolet-martin--curated-7.how: Tokenize the text, stream the tokens through the algorithm, and compare the estimate with an exact set-based count of the same stream.
steps: Collect a stream with a known exact cardinality.
Run the sketch over it.
Compare estimate with exact count.
Report the relative error alongside the memory used.

2q-cache.context: An analysis of LRU's failure on disk-backed database caches and the 2Q replacement algorithm from Johnson and Shasha, including Postgres's adoption.

2q-cache--curated-1.how: Add a probation queue in front of the LRU buffer so a page must be referenced twice before it can displace an admitted page.
steps: Identify scans or one-off reads in the workload.
Insert a probation stage before the main cache.
Promote only on a second reference.
Measure whether churn on the main buffer drops.

2q-cache--curated-2.how: Simulate a table scan larger than the buffer and track how many previously cached pages are evicted and never reused.
steps: Measure the buffer size and the largest table scan.
Replay a scan against the current policy.
Count evicted pages that are never re-read.
Add admission control if the loss is significant.

2q-cache--curated-3.how: Treat the first miss as an application to a probation list and require a hit there before granting space in the main LRU.
steps: Send every new page to probation.
Track hits while it waits there.
Promote on the second reference.
Discard pages that age out untouched.

2q-cache--curated-4.how: Implement `A1` as a FIFO list and `Am` as a hash map plus doubly linked list; move a page from `A1` to `Am` on a hit and evict from the tail of `A1` on a miss.
steps: Build the FIFO probation queue.
Build the LRU main buffer.
On a hit in probation, promote the page.
On a miss, evict the oldest probation entry.

2q-cache--curated-5.how: Size the probation queue against the observed reuse distance; too small forces an immediate second hit, too large leaves little room for admitted pages.
steps: Measure the reuse interval of warm pages.
Set the probation size from that interval.
Watch the promotion rate.
Resize when the working set changes.

2q-cache--curated-6.how: Keep `A1-In` for resident probation pages and `A1-Out` for identifiers of pages already evicted, so a later touch can still promote directly to `Am`.
steps: Split probation into resident and reference-only lists.
Insert new pages into the resident list.
Move identifiers to the reference list on eviction.
Promote to the main buffer on a reference-list hit.

2q-cache--curated-7.how: Postgres replaced ARC with 2Q after IBM's patent and reports comparable performance, making 2Q a patent-free substitute.
steps: Check whether your cache policy carries licensing constraints.
Evaluate 2Q against the incumbent on your workload.
Compare hit rate and overhead.
Switch only if performance holds.

israeli-queues.context: An introduction to Israeli Queues, a priority-queue variant from a 2007 polling-systems paper by Boxma, van der Wal, and Yechiali.

israeli-queues--curated-1.how: Change `enqueue` to accept a friend reference and insert the new element at the tail of that friend's group instead of assigning an explicit priority.
steps: Identify tasks with expensive shared setup.
Group tasks by that shared setup.
Enqueue each task with a reference to a group member.
Process groups rather than individual tasks.

israeli-queues--curated-2.how: Make the friend argument mandatory for grouped elements and optional for singletons; the insertion point, not a numeric field, carries the priority.
steps: Define `enqueue(element, friend)`.
Resolve the friend to its current group.
Insert at that group's tail.
Fall back to a new group at the rear.

israeli-queues--curated-3.how: Store groups in a doubly linked list and keep head and tail pointers per group; append at the group tail in O(1).
steps: Implement the queue as a doubly linked list.
Track each group's head and tail.
Append a friended element at the group tail.
Create a singleton group for elements without friends.
Optionally require the friend to be the group leader.

israeli-queues--curated-4.how: Track waiting time per ungrouped element and cap how long group-joining arrivals may delay it, or reserve service slots for singletons.
steps: Measure wait time for elements without friends.
Set a maximum acceptable delay.
Reserve periodic service for the oldest singleton group.
Alert when starvation crosses the threshold.

israeli-queues--curated-5.how: Dequeue an entire group and hand it to the worker as one unit when the setup cost is larger than the per-item processing time.
steps: Measure setup cost versus per-item cost.
Dequeue the full head group.
Process all its items under one setup.
Requeue the group only if new members arrived.

israeli-queues--curated-6.how: Model the server as visiting N queues cyclically and draining each queue's batch per visit, which is the polling-system pattern the structure generalizes.
steps: List the queues the server visits.
Measure the cost of visiting a queue.
Drain the whole batch per visit.
Move to the next queue in cycle.

1d-terrain.context: Part of a series on procedural-generation algorithms; the essay builds one-dimensional terrain from uniform noise, linear and cosine interpolation, and a weighted sum of sampled terrains, evaluated visually with Python plots.

1d-terrain--curated-1.how: Layer several noise signals whose sampling frequencies and weights change by powers of two, then normalize the weighted sum; the low-frequency layers carry the mountain silhouette and the high-frequency layer adds only small deviations.
steps: Generate one dense random height field as the base signal.
Create progressively sparser sampled versions of it.
Assign larger weights to the sparser versions.
Sum the weighted layers and normalize back to the height range.
Plot and compare against a real skyline before tuning.

1d-terrain--curated-2.how: Call the random generator independently at each x position, map the result from [0,1] to the desired height range, and plot. The lack of correlation between adjacent samples is what produces the spikes.
steps: Generate one independent uniform sample per x co-ordinate.
Map each sample to the target height interval.
Plot the series and inspect the change between adjacent points.
Compare it with a real terrain profile of the same length.

1d-terrain--curated-3.how: Implement a linear blend between two control points plus a cosine-eased variant that moves `mu` along a cosine curve. Both take the two known points and a relative position between them.
steps: Pick two known points a and b that bracket the gap.
Compute mu as the relative distance from a to the target point.
Use linear interpolation when straight segments are acceptable.
Use cosine interpolation when the seam at each control point is visible.

1d-terrain--curated-4.how: Take the naive terrain, keep every `sample`-th value as a control point, and interpolate the positions in between. Vary `sample` from 1 to 5 to see the smoothness tradeoff.
steps: Generate the dense random terrain.
Keep every k-th point as a control point.
Interpolate all skipped positions between consecutive controls.
Try k from 1 to 5 and compare the number of spikes.
Switch from linear to cosine interpolation for rounder transitions.

1d-terrain--curated-5.how: Six octaves with sample counts 256, 128, 64, 32, 16 and 8 received scales 0.03125, 0.0625, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0. The weighted sum was normalized to produce the final terrain.
steps: Choose an octave count; six covers most cases.
Halve the sample count for each successive octave.
Double the weight as the sample count halves.
Sum weight times terrain across all octaves.
Normalize the result and plot it against the target profile.

1d-terrain--curated-6.how: Build the generator as three composable functions: uniform terrain, interpolation over a sampling interval, and an octave combiner. Expose sample interval, interpolator, octave count and weight schedule as parameters.

jaccard-minhash.context: Part of a series on probabilistic data structures; the essay defines Jaccard similarity, derives the MinHash estimator, and tests the approximation on two equal-sized sets as they move from disjoint to identical.

jaccard-minhash--curated-1.how: Build a signature per set by applying k hash functions and keeping the minimum hash value under each, then compare signatures position by position. The match fraction estimates intersection over union without materializing either set.
steps: Tokenize each document or record into a set of shingles.
Choose k independent hash functions.
Compute the minimum hash under each function for every set.
Compare signature positions and divide matches by k.
Calibrate k against exact Jaccard on a small sample.

jaccard-minhash--curated-2.how: Compute `|A intersect B| / |A union B|` directly for small sets, and use the same ratio as the probability baseline when validating an approximate method.
steps: Represent both objects as finite sets.
Count the intersection and the union.
Divide intersection size by union size.
Use 0 and 1 as the disjoint and identical endpoints when sanity-checking.

jaccard-minhash--curated-3.how: Permute the universal set, then take the first element of the permutation that also belongs to S. Replace the permutation with a hash like `(a*x + b) mod c`, where a and b are below the universe size and c is a prime just above it.
steps: Define the universal set of all possible elements.
Pick a hash that permutes element IDs.
Hash every element of the set and keep the smallest value.
Repeat with independent hash functions to form a signature.

jaccard-minhash--curated-4.how: Each hash function contributes one minimum, so a signature of length k costs k passes over the set. Two sets are compared by counting equal positions and dividing by k.
steps: Choose k from the acceptable error, not from set size.
Generate k independent hash functions.
Store one minimum per function per set.
Compare equal positions and divide by k.
Increase k if the estimate is too noisy.

jaccard-minhash--curated-5.how: The error falls as k rises because each extra hash is another independent trial; the cost is one more hash pass and one more stored integer per set.
steps: Estimate the error your application can tolerate.
Start with a small k and measure against exact Jaccard.
Increase k until the error band is acceptable.
Account for the extra storage and hashing time.
Keep k fixed across sets so signatures stay comparable.

jaccard-minhash--curated-6.how: Two equal-cardinality disjoint sets were compared, then one element of the first set was replaced by an element of the second per step until the sets matched. Exact Jaccard and the MinHash estimate were plotted on the same axes.
steps: Create two disjoint sets of equal size.
Replace one element per step to move toward overlap.
Compute exact Jaccard at every step.
Compute the signature match rate at every step.
Plot both curves to see where the estimate drifts.

ts-smoothing.context: Part of a series on time-series analysis; the essay applies the ASAP smoothing method from Rong and Bailis to temperature and operational metrics, using kurtosis to pick a moving-average window that keeps anomalies visible.

ts-smoothing--curated-1.how: For each candidate window length, smooth the series with SMA, compute kurtosis on the result, and select the window with the highest kurtosis inside a bounded range.
steps: Define a plausible window range for the sampling cadence.
Smooth with SMA at each candidate length.
Compute kurtosis of every smoothed series.
Pick the in-range window with the highest kurtosis.
Check that known anomalies are still visible.

ts-smoothing--curated-2.how: Replace each point with a local mean instead of collapsing the series into coarse buckets; the x-axis keeps its original resolution and a spike still has neighbours to distort.
steps: Identify whether the current chart aggregates or averages.
Switch to a sliding window that retains every timestamp.
Compare where a known spike lands in both views.
Keep the representation that preserves its location and height.

ts-smoothing--curated-3.how: Slide a window of length n, average the values inside it, and emit one smoothed point per original timestamp. The essay demonstrates a window of 11 on a second time series.
steps: Choose an initial window length.
Average the values inside the rolling window.
Emit one output per input timestamp.
Compare the smoothed and raw plots side by side.

ts-smoothing--curated-4.how: Plot the same series at several window lengths and watch a known anomaly: small windows leave noise around it, while large windows flatten its peak and spread it across neighbours.
steps: Pick a series with a known anomaly.
Smooth it at several window lengths.
Measure the anomaly's peak height at each length.
Find where it stops being distinguishable from noise.
Treat that as the upper bound for the window.

ts-smoothing--curated-5.how: Kurtosis is the fourth standardized moment; adding a small amount of tail noise to a distribution raises it sharply, which makes it a usable objective for anomaly preservation.
steps: Compute kurtosis on the raw and smoothed series.
Compare a distribution with and without injected tail noise.
Confirm the tail noise produces a visible jump.
Use the statistic as the smoothing objective.

ts-smoothing--curated-6.how: Compute SMA for every window in a fixed interval, score each result with kurtosis, and take the local maximum. The essay bounds the search, for example from 10 to 40, instead of scanning every possible length.

lfu.context: Part of a series on caching and eviction; the essay reconstructs the O(1) LFU design from Shah, Mitra and Matani and contrasts it with heap-based LFU and LRU.

lfu--curated-1.how: Replace the heap with a hash table for key lookup, an ordered list of frequency nodes, and one value list per frequency. Every operation becomes a bounded set of pointer changes.
steps: Map each key to a value node in a hash table.
Keep frequency nodes in ascending order.
Attach each value node to its frequency node's list.
Update only pointers on hit, insert and evict.
Measure memory overhead against the heap version.

lfu--curated-2.how: Insert, hit and evict all change a frequency, and each change can violate heap order, so each operation triggers sift-up or sift-down work.
steps: Instrument how often a cache hit changes a frequency.
Count heap rebalancing operations per request.
Compare tail latency with an O(1) policy.
Decide whether the frequency signal is worth the log factor.

lfu--curated-3.how: KeyDir maps a key to a Value Node. The `freq_list` is sorted ascending; each Frequency Node stores `freq`, `next`, `prev` and `values_ptr`, and each Value Node stores `data`, list pointers and a `freq_pointer` back.
steps: Create the key-to-value hash table.
Create the sorted frequency list.
Give each frequency node a value list.
Add back-pointers from values to frequencies.
Draw the pointer graph before coding.

lfu--curated-4.how: Look up the value node, inspect its frequency node's successor, create a `freq + 1` node if missing, unlink the value from the old list and link it into the new one.
steps: Resolve the key to its value node.
Read the node's current frequency.
Check for a frequency node at freq + 1.
Create and splice it in if absent.
Move the value node and update its back-pointer.

lfu--curated-5.how: Insert checks for an existing key, ensures a frequency-1 node exists, wraps the value, appends it to that node's value list, and records the key in the hash table. Eviction takes the first value from the lowest-frequency node's list.
steps: Reject duplicate keys before inserting.
Ensure the frequency-1 node exists.
Append the new value to that node's list.
Evict from the head of the lowest-frequency list.
Update the key table on both paths.

lfu--curated-6.how: The RUM conjecture frames the choice: optimizing reads and updates costs memory. Every key, value node and frequency link stays resident, so capacity is bounded by RAM rather than disk.
steps: Estimate bytes per entry including node and pointer overhead.
Compare that with the cache's memory budget.
Measure the hit-rate gain over LRU.
Use LFU only where the gain justifies the footprint.
Shard by key if the working set exceeds one machine.

morris-counter.context: Part of a series on space-efficient algorithms; the essay walks through Morris's 1977 approximate counter, from a coin-flip halving trick to the logarithmic estimator used in small registers.

morris-counter--curated-1.how: Store a probabilistic encoding of the count rather than the count itself; the register only needs to reach about log n, so the storage needed is about log log n bits.
steps: Decide whether an approximate cardinality is acceptable.
Choose a register width for the required count range.
Use the probabilistic update rule instead of incrementing.
Report an estimate with its confidence interval.
Track relative error rather than absolute error.

morris-counter--curated-2.how: Flip a fair coin per event and increment only on heads; the register then holds roughly n/2, and doubling it estimates n. On an 8-bit register this extends the range from 256 to about 512.
steps: Increment on a fixed fraction p of events.
Divide the register value by p to estimate n.
Measure error at small and large n.
Note that relative error is worst at small counts.

morris-counter--curated-3.how: Encode the count as a value that grows logarithmically with n, so each register step covers a wider range as the count rises and the relative error stays roughly flat.
steps: Pick a logarithmic encoding for the register.
Derive the count estimate from the register value.
Verify the estimate grows fastest at small n.
Measure relative error across several magnitudes.

morris-counter--curated-4.how: Estimate n from v, compute the jump to the estimate for v + 1, set d to its reciprocal, draw r uniformly from [0,1), and increment only when r < d.
steps: Estimate n from the current register value.
Compute the estimate for v + 1.
Set d to the reciprocal of the difference.
Draw r uniformly and increment if r < d.
Verify the expected estimate advances by one event.

morris-counter--curated-5.how: The register needs log n states to represent n events, and log n states need log log n bits. The 95% band is twice the standard deviation on either side of the mean.
steps: Compute the register width needed for the target n.
Compare it with an exact counter's width.
Derive the estimator's standard deviation.
Quote a 95% interval around the estimate.
Test the interval against a simulated stream.

morris-counter--curated-6.how: Absolute error grows with n even as relative error stays stable, and individual runs vary, so the counter suits telemetry and per-item cardinalities rather than exact accounting.
steps: List where an exact count is contractually required.
Exclude those paths from approximate counting.
Use the counter for traffic and cardinality telemetry.
Expose the estimate with an error band.
Alert on the estimate's trend, not its exact value.

slowsort.context: Part of a series on algorithms; it explains the Multiply and Surrender paradigm behind Slowsort from Broder and Stolfi's 1986 pessimal-algorithms paper and contrasts it with Bogosort.

slowsort--curated-1.how: Study it as a control: every step is locally correct, but the recursion is arranged so the amount of work grows faster than any efficient sort's.
steps: Identify the progress each recursive step makes.
Compare it with the efficient algorithm it imitates.
Ask which step is doing the real work.
Use the contrast to explain the efficient design.

slowsort--curated-2.how: The pattern is visible in naive recursive Fibonacci: two recursive calls per level recompute the same subproblems, so the call tree grows exponentially while each individual call is correct.
steps: Draw the recursion tree for a small input.
Mark repeated subproblems.
Check whether memoization would remove them.
If yes, the code is accidentally Multiply and Surrender.

slowsort--curated-3.how: The in-place version sorts both halves, swaps the last elements so the larger is at the end, then calls itself on the first n minus one elements.
steps: Sort the left half recursively.
Sort the right half recursively.
Compare the two last elements and place the larger at the end.
Recurse on everything except that maximum.
Stop at a single element.

slowsort--curated-4.how: The recurrence combines two sorts of n/2 with one sort of n minus one and constant work; solving the lower bound gives a non-polynomial `n^log n`.
steps: Write the recurrence for the recursive calls.
Solve or bound it asymptotically.
Compare the result with n squared.
Plot measured runtimes to confirm the growth.

slowsort--curated-5.how: Bogosort permutes randomly and can move a nearly sorted array backwards; Slowsort's swaps only place elements in correct relative order, so its inversion count never increases.
steps: Track the inversion count during execution.
Check whether any step increases it.
Compare with a random-shuffle sort.
Use determinism and monotonic progress as the quality test.

bitcask.context: Part of a series on storage engines; the essay describes Bitcask, the append-only log plus in-memory index that backed Riak, and its read, write, delete and compaction paths.

bitcask--curated-1.how: Append each record to the active datafile and keep its location in KeyDir. The write path never seeks; the read path does one hash lookup and one positional read.
steps: Separate the append path from the lookup path.
Keep a memory-resident index of key locations.
Write only to the active file.
Read only the record the index points to.
Measure read and write latency separately.

bitcask--curated-2.how: Append a record containing `crc`, `timestamp`, `key_size`, `value_size`, key and value, then insert `file_id` and offset into KeyDir as one atomic step.
steps: Serialize the record with its checksum and sizes.
Append it to the active datafile.
Insert the key's file and offset into KeyDir.
Make both updates atomic.
Rotate the file when it hits the size threshold.

bitcask--curated-3.how: KeyDir gives the datafile and offset, the engine reads that record, verifies the CRC, and returns the value. Filesystem read-ahead can serve repeated reads.
steps: Look up the key in KeyDir.
Read the record at the stored offset.
Verify the CRC before returning.
Return the value without scanning other records.
Enable read-ahead for hot files.

bitcask--curated-4.how: An update appends the full new value and repoints the key; a delete appends a tombstone and removes the key from KeyDir. The old record remains until compaction.
steps: Append a new full record for an update.
Point KeyDir at the new offset.
Append a unique tombstone for a delete.
Remove the key from KeyDir.
Leave the dead record for compaction.

bitcask--curated-5.how: Walk immutable files, keep only the newest live record per key, write merged files with the same format, then atomically repoint the affected KeyDir entries.
steps: Scan immutable datafiles for live keys.
Keep only the latest version of each.
Write merged datafiles in the same format.
Update KeyDir offsets atomically.
Delete the superseded files.

bitcask--curated-6.how: For each datafile, write a hint file with keys and metadata but no values. At boot, rebuild KeyDir from hint files instead of reading every value.
steps: Emit a hint file alongside each datafile.
Store keys, sizes, timestamps and offsets.
Omit values entirely.
Rebuild KeyDir from hints on startup.
Fall back to a full scan if a hint is missing.

bitcask--curated-7.how: The key space is held in RAM for O(1) lookup; shard keys across multiple Bitcask instances when it outgrows one machine's memory.
steps: Measure the live key space and per-key overhead.
Compare it with available RAM after buffers.
Shard keys across instances before the ceiling.
Keep each shard's KeyDir independent.
Monitor memory as the key count grows.

phi-accrual.context: Part of a series on distributed-systems primitives; the essay explains the phi accrual failure detector from Hayashibara et al., which replaces a fixed heartbeat timeout with a continuous suspicion score.

phi-accrual--curated-1.how: Compute a suspicion value from the observed heartbeat interval distribution and expose it as a number. Each service maps its own threshold to the action it can tolerate.
steps: Replace the boolean timeout with a numeric suspicion score.
Publish the score from the detector.
Let each service choose its threshold.
Map thresholds to escalating actions.
Review thresholds against observed false positives.

phi-accrual--curated-2.how: A fixed timeout makes the tradeoff at configuration time: short means fast detection with false alarms, long means fewer false alarms with slow detection.
steps: Measure the real distribution of heartbeat intervals.
Set the timeout at a percentile, not a guess.
Track false positives and detection delay.
Re-evaluate when network conditions change.
Compare with an adaptive detector.

phi-accrual--curated-3.how: Estimate the probability that the next heartbeat arrives after the current silence, then compute `phi = -log10(P)`. The sign and scale make larger phi mean stronger suspicion.
steps: Estimate the tail probability of the current silence.
Apply `-log10` to that probability.
Track phi over time.
Set thresholds where the score becomes actionable.
Confirm phi accrues when heartbeats stop.

phi-accrual--curated-4.how: Keep a sliding window of arrival times, derive inter-arrival intervals, compute mean and variance, treat the intervals as normal, and integrate the density from the elapsed time to infinity.
steps: Record arrival timestamps in a sliding window.
Compute inter-arrival intervals.
Estimate their mean and variance.
Integrate the normal tail beyond the current gap.
Feed the probability into the phi formula.

phi-accrual--curated-5.how: Because phi is logarithmic, threshold X corresponds to roughly 10^-X probability that the suspicion is wrong. Different thresholds can trigger probe, warn and failover.
steps: Translate each threshold into a false-suspicion budget.
Use a low threshold for probing.
Use a high threshold for failover.
Keep the action policy in the application.
Audit decisions against late heartbeats.

decipher-repeated-key-xor.context: Part of a series of cryptography essays working through the Cryptopals challenges; this one breaks repeating-key XOR from Set 1 Challenge 6 using Hamming distance and frequency analysis.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-1.how: Align ciphertext bytes produced by the same key position, XOR them together so the key cancels, and measure whether the result looks like English-to-English XOR rather than random bytes.
steps: Assume the key repeats at some unknown period.
Compare ciphertext positions at that offset.
XOR pairs to cancel the shared key byte.
Score the result for English-like closeness.
Pick the period with the strongest signal.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-2.how: Repeat the key to the plaintext length, XOR byte by byte, and treat the output as a byte string. Decryption calls the same function on the ciphertext.
steps: Convert plaintext and key to bytes.
Repeat the key to the plaintext length.
XOR each plaintext byte with its key byte.
Store the result as raw bytes.
Decrypt by running the same XOR again.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-3.how: XOR two equal-length byte strings, count the set bits in each result byte, sum them, and divide by the number of bit pairs. Lowercase English pairs average about 2.45 bits versus about 3.9999 for random bytes.
steps: XOR the two byte strings.
Count set bits in every resulting byte.
Sum the counts for the distance.
Divide by total bit pairs for the score.
Calibrate against known English and random samples.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-4.how: For each candidate length, split the ciphertext into that many chunks, average the Hamming score of corresponding chunks, and look for a minimum. Lengths that are multiples of the key produce the same dip.
steps: Choose a range of candidate key lengths.
Chunk the ciphertext at each length.
Average Hamming scores across corresponding chunks.
Plot score against length.
Take the minimum and check its multiples.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-5.how: Treat each key position as a single-byte XOR: try all 256 candidates for that column, score the decrypted bytes with letter frequencies and a fitting quotient, and keep the best.
steps: Slice the ciphertext into key-length columns.
Try all 256 byte keys per column.
Score each candidate with English letter frequencies.
Keep the highest-scoring byte per column.
Concatenate the bytes into the key.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-6.how: The test encrypted 100 random English sentences with random keys of varying length, then ran key-length detection and frequency scoring. The pipeline recovered 99.
steps: Build a test set of random English sentences.
Encrypt each with a random key length.
Run the detector and scorer.
Compare recovered text with the original.
Inspect the one failure for a pattern.

decipher-repeated-key-xor--curated-7.how: The score depends on plaintext bytes occupying a narrow range; binary, compressed or already-encrypted data removes that signal, and multiples of the period can score equally low.
steps: Check that the plaintext is likely natural language.
Do not apply this to compressed or encrypted payloads.
Inspect several low-scoring lengths, not just one.
Decrypt with each candidate and score the text.
Reject results that fail a readability check.

decipher-single-xor.context: Part of a series working through the Cryptopals challenges, covering Set 1 Challenge 3: recovering a plaintext encrypted with a single-byte XOR key. The code is in a notebook at arpitbhayani.me/decipher-single-byte-xor.

decipher-single-xor--curated-1.how: Treat the unknown key as a search variable: decrypt with each of the 256 byte values, score the output for English-likeness, and return the best-scoring plaintext. The essay wraps the whole loop in one function.
steps: Confirm the cipher uses one key byte, so the key space is exactly 256.
Write a decrypt routine that XORs every ciphertext byte with a candidate key.
Define a score that measures distance from English letter frequencies.
Loop over every key and retain the minimum score.
Read the recovered text to confirm it is not a coincidental near-miss.

decipher-single-xor--curated-2.how: Implement a single function that XORs each byte of the input with the key and call it for both directions; no separate decryption path is needed.
steps: Write one byte-wise XOR function that takes data and a key.
Use it unchanged for encryption.
Pass the ciphertext through the same function to decrypt.
Test with a known pair such as `abcd` and key `69`.

decipher-single-xor--curated-3.how: Iterate the key over `range(0, 256)`, decrypt, compute a score for each candidate, and keep the argmin rather than inspecting outputs by hand.
steps: Generate the full candidate set instead of guessing likely keys.
Decrypt every candidate to a plaintext string.
Score all candidates with the same function.
Return the single lowest-scoring candidate.

decipher-single-xor--curated-4.how: Use published English letter frequencies as the reference distribution, for example `a` at 8.239% and `b` at 1.505%, with the twelve most common letters summarised as ETAOIN SHRDLU.
steps: Collect a reference frequency table for the target language.
Compute the candidate text's own letter distribution.
Compare the two distributions rather than eyeballing the text.
Restrict the comparison to the alphabet and ignore punctuation.

decipher-single-xor--curated-5.how: Compute per-letter relative frequencies for the candidate, subtract the English percentages, take absolute values, and average them across letters. The key with the smallest average wins.
steps: Normalise the candidate text to lowercase letters.
Compute the percentage of each letter in the candidate.
Sum the absolute differences from the reference percentages.
Divide by the number of letters compared.
Rank all 256 keys by that quotient.

decipher-single-xor--curated-6.how: The essay validated the scorer on 100 random English sentences with random keys, and noted that very short or symbol-dense inputs fall outside what the frequency table can represent.
steps: Check plaintext length before trusting a frequency-based result.
Strip or account for symbols that are not letters.
Treat a low-confidence score as ambiguous rather than correct.
Fall back to manual review or more ciphertext when the sample is tiny.

python-iterable-integers.context: Part of a Python internals series that modifies CPython to see how the language works; related essays cover super-long integers and the integer cache.

python-iterable-integers--curated-1.how: Patch CPython: add a `long_iter` function, register it on the `tp_iter` slot of `PyLong_Type`, rebuild the binary, and compare iteration behaviour against the stock build.
steps: Locate the type object for integers in `longobject.c`.
Check which slot controls iteration for that type.
Add a slot function that returns an iterator.
Rebuild CPython and run `for x in 7`.
Test unrelated syntax such as tuple unpacking for regressions.

python-iterable-integers--curated-2.how: Implement `__iter__` to return an object whose `__next__` yields values and raises `StopIteration` when exhausted; that pair is the entire contract the `for` loop relies on.
steps: Write an iterator class with a `__next__` method.
Raise `StopIteration` when there is nothing left.
Have `__iter__` return that iterator.
Verify the object works in a `for` loop and in `list()`.

python-iterable-integers--curated-3.how: Read the `PyTypeObject` definition for a built-in type and note which function-pointer slots are filled and which are `NULL`; the empty `tp_iter` on `PyLong_Type` is what blocks iteration.
steps: Find the `PyTypeObject` instance for the type you care about.
List which operation slots are non-NULL.
Identify the slot that corresponds to the Python dunder.
Treat a NULL slot as an intentional capability gap, not necessarily an oversight.

python-iterable-integers--curated-4.how: Add `PyLongRangeIter_ZeroToN` in `rangeobject.c`, declare it in `rangeobject.h`, and have `long_iter` return its `longrangeiterobject` with start 0, end n and step 1.
steps: Write a helper that builds a range iterator from an integer.
Declare the helper in the matching header.
Implement the slot function to call the helper with the integer.
Assign the function to `tp_iter` on the integer type.
Rebuild and confirm `for x in 7` yields 0 through 6.

python-iterable-integers--curated-5.how: After the patch, `a, b = 7` iterates the integer into seven values and fails, while `a, b = 2` succeeds. The asymmetry appears purely because the right-hand side is now treated as a sequence.
steps: Write a two-target unpacking statement against a small integer.
Compare the result for a value below and above the target count.
Note that the failure is a `ValueError`, not a `TypeError`.
Trace unpacking back to iteration to explain the change.

python-iterable-integers--curated-6.how: Reason from the language's existing contract: unpacking consumes any iterable on the right, and integers are exempt only because they are singular. Making them iterable changes assignments that currently read as scalars.
steps: List the syntax that consumes an iterable implicitly.
Identify where a scalar is currently assumed.
Check whether a proposed type change alters those sites.
Prefer a new wrapper type over changing a built-in's protocol.

inheritance-c.context: Part of a systems-internals series on code reuse at the C level; the struct definitions are taken from the Linux kernel and CPython's object model.

inheritance-c--curated-1.how: Define the shared fields in a parent struct, embed that struct as the first member of each variant, and cast child pointers to the parent type wherever shared logic is applied.
steps: Extract the fields every variant shares into a parent struct.
Embed the parent as the first member of each child struct.
Cast child pointers to the parent type at call sites.
Write shared operations only against the parent type.
Verify member offsets after any layout change.

inheritance-c--curated-2.how: Declare the inner struct as a plain member, not a pointer, so its bytes are part of the outer allocation. `list_int` holds a `list_head` plus an `int`; `list_str` holds the same head plus a `char *`.
steps: Separate the reusable fields from the payload fields.
Declare the reusable struct as a value member.
Add the payload after it.
Access the shared fields through the member name.

inheritance-c--curated-3.how: Cast a `list_int *` to `list_head *` and use the result directly; the parent occupies the first bytes, so no adjustment is required.
steps: Confirm the parent is the first declared member.
Cast the child pointer to the parent pointer type.
Pass the cast pointer to functions that only need shared fields.
Avoid casting back unless you know the concrete child type.

inheritance-c--curated-4.how: Print the addresses of each member of a composed struct to confirm they occupy one contiguous block in declaration order, with the parent at the lowest offset.
steps: Take the address of the outer struct and of each member.
Compare the offsets to the declaration order.
Check the total size against the sum of the members.
Re-run the check on every target architecture you support.

inheritance-c--curated-5.how: Implement `__list_add`, delete, splice, rotate and swap to take `list_head *`. Any struct embedding the head can be passed without a wrapper or a vtable.
steps: Identify operations that touch only the shared fields.
Change their signatures to the parent pointer type.
Keep payload-specific logic in separate functions.
Call the shared operations with a cast child pointer.
Add a new child type without touching the shared code.

inheritance-c--curated-6.how: CPython places `PyObject` first in every object struct, so reference counting is implemented once against `PyObject *`. The Linux kernel does the same with `list_head` for list membership.
steps: Define a header struct with the fields every object needs.
Embed it first in each concrete type.
Write bookkeeping routines against the header type only.
Free or mutate through the concrete type.
Audit that no object struct places the header anywhere but first.

rum.context: A summary of the research paper Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture, which proposes a CAP-like trade-off for storage engines.

rum--curated-1.how: Classify a candidate engine by which corner it optimizes, then measure the other two costs rather than assuming they are acceptable.
steps: Write down the workload's read, update and space profile.
Identify which of the three the engine is tuned for.
Measure the amplification it imposes on the other two.
Reject engines whose weak corner matches your dominant workload.
Re-evaluate when the workload mix changes.

rum--curated-2.how: Instrument the engine to count bytes read, written and stored, then divide each by the bytes of main data the query actually needed.
steps: Define what counts as main data versus auxiliary data.
Measure total bytes read per query.
Measure total bytes written per update.
Measure allocated space including indexes and deltas.
Track the three ratios over time, not just at peak load.

rum--curated-3.how: Read-optimized systems keep hash or tree indexes in front of the data. Estimate the index maintenance cost per write and the read penalty once updates start arriving faster than the index can absorb them cheaply.
steps: Count auxiliary probes per read.
Count auxiliary writes per update.
Estimate the read slowdown at your update rate.
Prefer this family for read-dominant, slowly changing data.

rum--curated-4.how: Update-optimized systems buffer changes in a delta area and merge them in bulk. Budget for the extra read path that must consult several tiers and pick the winning version.
steps: Measure how many tiers a point read must consult.
Account for conflict resolution in read latency.
Track disk space held by unmerged tiers.
Schedule compaction against write bursts, not just timers.
Prefer this family for write-heavy ingestion.

rum--curated-5.how: Memory-optimized systems use compression, sparse indexes or probabilistic structures. Quantify the false-positive rate and the encode/decode cost before adopting one.
steps: Decide which error rate the query can tolerate.
Measure the space saved against the exact structure.
Add compression and decompression to read and write latency.
Check how many extra records a lookup must scan.
Keep the structure only where the saved space pays for that work.

rum--curated-6.how: A clustered index stores rows in the index's leaf pages, so a lookup that finds the page has the data already; no second fetch against main storage is needed.
steps: Check whether the index is clustered or secondary.
Count the fetches a single lookup requires.
Prefer clustering for range scans over the clustering key.
Account for the write cost of keeping rows ordered.

consistent-hashing.context: An explainer that builds consistent hashing from the modulo approach using two sorted arrays and binary search. The implementation is at github.com/arpitbbhayani/consistent-hashing.

consistent-hashing--curated-1.how: Start from `hash(key) % N`, then count how many keys change owner when N changes. Consistent hashing replaces the modulus with a fixed space and a successor rule.
steps: Record the current key-to-node mapping.
Add one node and recompute with the new modulus.
Count how many keys moved.
Compare that churn with the capacity you gained.
Adopt a placement scheme whose churn scales with the node, not the dataset.

consistent-hashing--curated-2.how: Hash the same five sample keys with `mod 5` and `mod 7` and compare the resulting node indices. The essay's mapping goes from E, A, B, C, D to D, E, F, G, A.
steps: Pick a representative set of keys.
Compute their owners under the old node count.
Recompute under the new count.
Count the differing assignments.
Use that number to estimate migration cost at production scale.

consistent-hashing--curated-3.how: Hash nodes and keys into the same fixed space, then assign each key to the first node at or after its position, wrapping around at the end.
steps: Choose a hash function with a large, fixed output space.
Hash every node into that space.
Hash the key into the same space.
Walk clockwise to the first node.
Wrap to the smallest node when you pass the end.

consistent-hashing--curated-4.how: Maintain `keys` and `nodes` in parallel, sorted by key, with a one-to-one correspondence. Use binary search for the first key greater than the item's hash and return the node at that index, or index 0.
steps: Store node positions in a sorted array.
Store node identities in a parallel array.
Binary search for the successor position on lookup.
Return the matching node, wrapping to zero when needed.
Insert and delete in both arrays at the same index.

consistent-hashing--curated-5.how: Insert the new node at its hashed position, find the successor with binary search, and copy only the keys in the arc between the new node's predecessor and the new node from that successor.
steps: Hash the new node to get its ring position.
Binary search for the successor's index.
Identify the arc the new node will own.
Copy that arc's keys from the successor.
Insert the node into both sorted arrays.

consistent-hashing--curated-6.how: Binary search the departing node's index, transfer its keys to the next node to the right, then remove the entry from both arrays and shift the tail.
steps: Find the departing node's index by binary search.
Identify its clockwise successor.
Move the departing node's keys to the successor.
Delete the position and identity from both arrays.
Confirm the ring still wraps correctly at the end.

consistent-hashing--curated-7.how: Compare the literal array-of-hash-space design, which allocates one slot per possible hash, against the compressed sorted-array design, which stores only node positions.
steps: Estimate memory for one slot per hash value.
Estimate lookup cost for a linear walk to the next node.
Replace the dense array with a sorted list of node positions.
Use binary search for the successor instead of walking.

python-caches-integers.context: Part of a Python internals series; it follows an essay on how CPython represents arbitrarily large integers.

python-caches-integers--curated-1.how: Read the `PyLongObject` definition to see the digit array, then look at `IS_SMALL_INT` and `get_small_int` in `longobject.c` to see how the -5 to 256 range bypasses allocation.
steps: Find the integer struct definition in `longobject.c`.
Note how digits are stored and how size is encoded.
Locate the small-integer macros and helpers.
Compare allocation paths inside and outside the range.
Benchmark a small-int-heavy loop against a large-int one.

python-caches-integers--curated-2.how: The value is stored as digits in base 2^30, so the digit count grows with magnitude. Arithmetic therefore involves per-digit work and allocation rather than a single machine instruction.
steps: Inspect `sys.getsizeof` for integers of increasing magnitude.
Observe the step changes as digit count grows.
Time arithmetic on small versus very large values.
Account for that cost when choosing Python for numeric hot loops.

python-caches-integers--curated-3.how: At startup CPython instantiates every integer from -5 through 256 once. Later references return the existing object, which is why those values behave as shared singletons.
steps: Confirm the documented range in the language reference.
Check the `IS_SMALL_INT` condition in the source.
See where `get_small_int` returns the cached object.
Note that the range is fixed, not configurable at runtime.

python-caches-integers--curated-4.how: Call `id()` on two variables bound to the same small value and compare the addresses; repeat for values above 256 and for two computations that reach the same small result.
steps: Bind two names to the same small integer.
Compare their `id` values.
Repeat with a value above 256.
Compute the same result by two different expressions.
Compare the resulting identities.

python-caches-integers--curated-5.how: The cached range stops at 256, so a fresh object is allocated for larger results. Verify by comparing addresses of equal large values produced by separate expressions.
steps: Produce the same large value twice by separate operations.
Compare their addresses.
Replace identity checks with value equality in numeric code.
Audit code that relies on interned constants.

python-caches-integers--curated-6.how: Iterate over the range -5 to 300, call `sys.getrefcount` on each value in a fresh interpreter, and plot the counts. The resulting curve peaks at 0 and shows spikes at powers of two.
steps: Start a fresh interpreter to avoid your own references.
Measure `getrefcount` across the range of interest.
Plot the distribution rather than sampling a few values.
Look for spikes at powers of two.
Compare total allocations with and without preallocation.

fractional-cascading.context: An algorithms essay that derives fractional cascading from the cost of repeated binary searches and implements it in Python. The code is at github.com/arpitbbhayani/fractional-cascading.

fractional-cascading--curated-1.how: Precompute, for each element of each list, where its neighbours land in the next list. Then search only the top list and follow those links downward with constant work per level.
steps: Measure the cost of independent searches first.
Decide which lists to link and in what order.
Precompute the cross-list positions.
Search the top list once.
Follow links for the remaining lists.

fractional-cascading--curated-2.how: Call `bisect_left` on each of the k lists for the same target and collect the returned indices. That gives the reference time and space costs to compare against.
steps: Implement the straightforward k-search version.
Use `bisect_left` for the successor position in each list.
Record runtime as k grows.
Record memory use as a baseline.

fractional-cascading--curated-3.how: Merge all elements into one sorted auxiliary array and attach a k-item position tuple to each. One binary search then returns every list's index, at the cost of storing k integers per element.
steps: Build the merged sorted array.
Compute each element's position in all k lists.
Store the tuple alongside the element.
Binary search the merged array once.
Read the answer from the matching tuple.

fractional-cascading--curated-4.how: Construct `M(k-1)` from the last original list, then build each higher level as the merge of its original list and every second element of the level below.
steps: Start at the deepest list.
Take every other element from the level below.
Merge those with the current original list.
Keep the result sorted.
Repeat upward until the top level exists.

fractional-cascading--curated-5.how: Store two integers per auxiliary element: its index in the original list at that level, and its index in the auxiliary list one level down.
steps: Binary search the original list for each element's position.
Binary search the lower auxiliary list for the same element.
Store both indices together.

Rebuild and compare the patched binary against the original.

i-changed-my-python--curated-2.how: Build the randomized branch and evaluate `4 + 6` repeatedly; the operator changes between runs because the pick comes from the clock.
steps: Run the same addition several times in one session.
Record each result and map it back to an operator.
Confirm the distribution changes across sessions.
Use the mapping to verify that all branches are reachable.

steps: Disassemble `a + b` to see `BINARY_ADD`.
Read the evaluation loop case for opcode 23.
Confirm the operand stack order before and after the operation.
Guard the patch so non-numeric operands take the normal path.

steps: List the `PyNumber_*` functions you want in the pool.
Seed a choice from the current epoch second.
Write one helper that takes two operands and an operator index.
Call the helper from the opcode case instead of the fixed add.

steps: Run the build and read where it crashes.
Check whether the patched function is reachable before the REPL starts.
Assume every core operation has non-interactive callers.
Gate the change on the caller rather than removing the patch.

Add a `source` argument to the functions on the call chain.

fast-and-efficient-pagination-in-mongodb.context: First of three posts on MongoDB pagination, followed by a note on why `skip` is slow and a benchmark of both approaches.

fast-and-efficient-pagination-in-mongodb.how: Two cursor strategies: `skip` plus `limit` uses an offset, while `_id` plus `limit` uses the last seen id as a lower bound.
steps: Write down how deep your pages actually go.
Compare an offset query with a range query on `_id`.
Check the plan each one uses.
Pick the shape that matches your page depth.

fast-and-efficient-pagination-in-mongodb.how: `find()` returns a cursor; `skip(page × size)` then `limit(size)` returns one page, with the server discarding the skipped documents.
steps: Compute the offset as page index times page size.
Apply `skip` and `limit` to the same cursor.
Run it in the Mongo shell and again from the driver.
Check the response time as the page index grows.

fast-and-efficient-pagination-in-mongodb.how: Read the 12-byte `ObjectId` layout, then compare ids with `<` and `>` in the Mongo shell to see the ordering.
steps: Break an `ObjectId` into its four fields.
Sort a small collection by `_id`.
Compare two ids numerically and lexically.
Confirm `_id` has a default index.

fast-and-efficient-pagination-in-mongodb.how: Keep the last document's `_id` from the current page and filter the next query on `_id > last_id` with the same limit.
steps: Fetch the first page and take its final `_id`.
Filter the next query to ids greater than that value.
Apply the same page size as the first request.
Check the plan to confirm the `_id` index is used.

mongodb-cursor-skip-is-slow.context: Second post in a three-part series on MongoDB pagination, between the two-approach overview and the benchmark.

mongodb-cursor-skip-is-slow--curated-1.how: MongoDB's `skip` documentation warns that skipped documents are iterated, and the implementation shows no index lookup to jump ahead.
steps: Read the warning attached to `cursor.skip`.
Time a shallow page and a deep page of the same query.
Show that the delay grows with the offset.
Trace the skip path in the server source.

mongodb-cursor-skip-is-slow--curated-2.how: Add an index and re-time a deep page; the skip portion stays expensive because it does not use the index to advance.
steps: Benchmark a deep page before adding an index.
Add an index on the filter field.
Re-run the same page fetch.
Attribute the remaining cost to the skip, not the lookup.

mongodb-cursor-skip-is-slow--curated-3.how: Time the same page fetch at shallow and deep offsets on a small collection to find where the skip cost becomes noticeable.
steps: Measure a page near the start of the result set.
Measure the same page size near the end.
Compare the two on your own data volume.
Switch to a range query only where the difference shows.

benchmark-and-compare-pagination-approac.context: Third post in a three-part MongoDB pagination series, benchmarking the two approaches introduced in the overview.

benchmark-and-compare-pagination-approac.how: Page through an unindexed collection with both approaches at a fixed page size, timing every page and plotting response time against collection size.
steps: Build a collection large enough to cross a few hundred documents.
Run both query shapes at the same page size.
Plot page time against collection size.
Mark where the two curves separate.

benchmark-and-compare-pagination-approac.how: Each page was fetched three times and averaged, with page size held fixed; the run was repeated on different machines and disks.
steps: Hold page size constant across both approaches.
Repeat each page fetch and average the timings.
Run the sweep on more than one machine or disk.
Check that the curve shape repeats.

benchmark-and-compare-pagination-approac.how: Use the measured crossover: comparable below about 500-600 documents, keyset clearly better beyond it; page sizes above 100 narrow the gap.
steps: Estimate the largest result set you will page through.
Compare it with the crossover on your own hardware.
Default to the simpler offset query below it.
Test larger page sizes if you need the simpler query at scale.

benchmark-and-compare-pagination-approac.how: Re-run anomalous pages and compare runs across disks before attributing a spike to the query strategy.
steps: Mark samples that sit above the trend line.
Re-run those exact page fetches.
Repeat the run on a different disk.
Discard the spike if it does not reproduce.

steps: Send a `GET` with no parameters and read the body.
